1 Hamim: water of extreme heat and scalding.

2 The Qur'an has shown that believers, despite their obedience to Allah, are anxious about the Day of Resurrection and its terrors. This is due to the greatness of their faith, their belief that Allah is swift in reckoning and severe in punishment, and because they perform acts of obedience while fearing they will not be accepted, and they fall into sins while fearing He will not forgive them. He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Those who fear their Lord in the unseen, and they are apprehensive of the Hour﴾ (al-Anbiya', 49).

3 The words of the Most High, ﴿yarji'un﴾, occur in six places in the Noble Qur'an: Al 'Imran (83), al-An'am (36), Maryam (40), al-Nur (64), al-Qasas (39), and Ghafir (77).

4 Yudda'un: are pushed with a violent push. Al-da'([d]a'): expulsion and pushing. The Most High said: ﴿Then that is the one who repulses the orphan (2)﴾ (al-Ma'un).

5 Al-zabad: is what rises on the surface of sea water when its waves become agitated. A sea that is "muzbid" is one whose waves are churning, casting up foam. The foam of water is its scum and filth. Plural: azbad.

6 Rabiyan: elevated, because it is on the highest surface of the water.

7 Jufa' al-sayl: is what the torrent throws up of foam, dirt, and the like.

8 Root: "raja'a" from the pattern "daraba": yarji'u, rujuan. "Raja'a" means to return to a place from which one had started; it is intransitive. "Rajja'ahu" means someone else caused it to return and restored it; it is transitive by itself. "Raja'a basarahu" means he looked again and again. From the intransitive is the words of the Most High: ﴿And when Musa returned to his people...﴾ (al-A'raf, 150), that is, he came back. From the transitive: ﴿So if Allah returns you to a group of them...﴾ (al-Tawbah, 83), that is, He restores and sends you back. From the figurative is His words: ﴿Then return the gaze twice...﴾ (al-Mulk, 4). Al-Qamus al-Qawim, pp. 256-257.

9 "Dallalna fi al-ard" means: our traces went away in the earth and we became hidden because of the dissolution of our bodies.

10 Al-judhman: the body. The Most High said: ﴿So they were found in their homes, lying prostrate﴾ (Hud, 67), that is, bodies lying upon the earth.

11 Al-nushur: the raising of the dead on the Day of Resurrection. The Most High said: ﴿Then when He wills, He will raise him﴾ (Abasa, 22), that is, He will give him life and raise him. And He said: ﴿To Him is the resurrection﴾ (al-Mulk, 15). From it comes "al-nushur": the Day of Resurrection.

The question of resurrection and rising is one of four main issues that the disbelievers denied, and the Qur'an recounts their words: ﴿And they said: when we are bones and fragments, shall we indeed be resurrected as a new creation?﴾ (al-Isra', 49). He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And he sets forth for Us a parable and forgets his own creation. He says: who will give life to bones when they are decayed? Say: He who produced them the first time will give them life, and He is Knowing of every creation﴾ (Ya Sin, 78-79).

12 In this regard, He, glory be to Him and exalted, says: ﴿Does man think he will be left neglected?﴾ (al-Qiyamah, 36). Ibn Zayd and Mujahid said: does the son of Adam think that he will be left neglected, neither believing nor being forbidden? It was also said: does man think that he will be left in his grave like that forever, never to be resurrected? Mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (10/7152).

13 "A'ya al-insan bi amr": he was unable to do it.

14 Al-labs: the confusion of a matter, and doubt.

15 The uproar of the philosophers arose from doubts and suppositions that developed in their minds regarding the impossibility of resurrection after death. They gave examples that they imagined supported their corrupt view, among them: someone eaten by fish and sea animals, or eaten by a lion or wild beasts. These doubts are based on what His Eminence the Shaykh mentioned on page 5714 about the doctrine of the philosophers, that Allah created the universe and then left its elements to interact according to their own inherent laws, meaning that Allah has no sustaining authority over His universe. The Qur'an has clearly refuted these doubts with the words of Allah, glory be to Him, about His creation of this universe, His sustaining authority over it, and His knowledge that encompasses every detail of the universe, so that not even an atom's weight escapes Him. He, glory be to Him, is the All-Powerful, from whose power nothing escapes. Since Allah created the universe from nothing, its restoration after its annihilation is easier for Him, glory be to Him. He, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿And it is He who originates creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ (al-Rum, 27). And He, exalted, says: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah, when you were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then give you life again, then to Him you will be returned﴾ (al-Baqarah, 28).

16 Rabat: became great, swelled, and increased.

17 Al-taqtir: purification and clarification from foreign harmful substances that may adhere to it.
Al-taqtir: converting a liquid into vapor by heat and then cooling it so it returns to liquid as it was, by means of a distillation apparatus (al-Mu'jam al-Wasit).

Al-Bukhari (?) — no, I'll translate only the given text.

Here is the translation:

Al-bukhar (vapour): everything that rises like smoke from hot liquids (al-Mu'jam al-Wasit). Tabkhir al-ma' (evaporation of water): heating it until it changes into its gaseous state and rises in the form of vapour.

18. Al-takthif (condensation): exposing water vapour to a cold surface so that it condenses on it, cools, and returns to its liquid state (by means of a distillation apparatus).

19. Natah (transpiration): oozing. It is said: nataja al-'araq 'an al-jild (sweat oozed from the skin), nataja al-ina' bi-ma fihi (the vessel exuded what was in it), and nataha al-harr (the heat caused it to exude). Water exudes from plants: natahan, meaning the excess water exits from them beyond their need (al-Mu'jam al-Wasit, with adaptation).

20. Al-dhariyat: the winds. Dharat al-rih al-turab wa ghayrahu tadhruhu dharwan: the wind lifted and carried away the dust and other things. The Exalted said: ﴿The winds scatter it﴾ (al-Kahf 45). Al-hamilat wiqran: the clouds. Al-jariyat yusran: the ships. Al-muqassimat amran: the angels.

It is established from Imam 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) that he ascended the pulpit of Kufa and said: "Do not ask me about any verse in the Book of Allah the Exalted, or about any sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), except that I will inform you of it." Ibn al-Kawwa' stood up and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, what is the meaning of the words of the Exalted: ﴿By those that scatter, scattering﴾ (al-Dhariyat 1)?" 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The wind." He said: "﴿And those that carry a load﴾ (2)?" He said: "The clouds." He said: "﴿And those that run with ease﴾ (3)?" He said: "The ships." He said: "﴿And those that distribute a command﴾ (4)?" He, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The angels." (Mentioned by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir, 4/231.)

21. Every disclosure is one of the secrets of His unseen, glory be to Him, and it has an hour of birth in which the Creator manifests Himself to everyone who deals with the universe through research, contemplation and benefit. As long as the Qur'an remains eternal, the flow of disclosure will continue to arrive, and in its arrival there is benefit, toward the meaning of the words of the Truth: ﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as a supplement﴾ (al-Kahf 109).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 10, verse 5:

Then the Truth (al-Haqq), glory be to Him, says:

﴿He it is Who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light, and determined for it stages, that you might know the number of years and the reckoning. Allah did not create that except in truth. He details the signs for a people who know.﴾ (10:5)

Having shown that the Truth created the heavens and the earth, and created the whole cosmos and subjected it to man, He mentions some of His blessings among His signs which He created for us, and which Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, made a cause for the sustenance (qiwam) of life. The sun is what ripens for us everything in existence, and gives every being its own particular radiance. Likewise, the sun evaporates the waters, as we said before, so that water descends afterwards sweet and fresh (furat), from which man drinks, livestock drink, and with which we irrigate crops.

The sun is the mother of a group of planets that revolve around it. The revolution of the earth around the sun represents the year, and the revolution of the earth around itself represents the day. Here Allah, glory be to Him, says:

﴿He it is Who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light﴾. If you look at the surface meaning of the sun and the moon, you would say: the sun gives light, and the moon likewise gives light. But a deeper look requires you to distinguish between the two: the sun gives radiance (ḍiyāʾ), and the moon gives light (nūr). The difference between ḍiyāʾ and nūr is that ḍiyāʾ is accompanied by heat and warmth, while nūr is a gentle illumination (ināra ḥalīma); for this reason the light of the moon is called the "gentle light." You do not need shade to protect yourself from its heat, whereas the sun requires a shelter to protect you from its heat.

Therefore: nūr is a light that has no heat in it, and heat only arises when the light is intrinsic to the luminous body, as with the sun. As for the moon, its light is not intrinsic; it acquires its light from the rays of the sun when they are reflected upon it. It is like a mirror: when some light is cast upon it, it reflects it.

Therefore: the moon is luminous by other than itself, whereas the sun shines by itself. For this reason the Truth said here: ﴿made the sun a radiance and the moon a light﴾.

The word ﴿ḍiyāʾ﴾ may be taken as a singular, like ṣāma ṣiyāman, qāma qiyāman, ḍāʾa ḍiyāʾan. Or it may be taken as a plural, like ḥawḍ (plural ḥiyāḍ) and rawḍ (plural riyāḍ); likewise the plural of ḍawʾ (light) is ḍiyāʾ.

Therefore the word ﴿ḍiyāʾ﴾ is suitable to be a plural and suitable to be a singular. When a word comes that is suitable both for the plural and the singular, the eloquent speaker must have a purpose in it, because it bears all these meanings. Before our knowledge of the secrets of sunlight and before its analysis, we used to say: it is light (ḍawʾ). But after we analysed sunlight, we found that the colours of the spectrum are seven, among them red light, green light, yellow light and others.

Therefore: "ḍiyāʾ" expresses the multiplicity of colours stored within the sun's radiance. If you say ḍiyāʾ is the plural of ḍawʾ, this is by analysing the light into all its components; if you say ḍiyāʾ is like qiyām and ṣiyām, this suits the general meaning.

This is why the Qur'an descended in a manner that the minds of its contemporaries could bear, minds that did not know the scientific meanings of phenomena. Had the Qur'an stated these realities, someone would have said: "I see the sun red at the moment of sunset and I see it yellow at midday," not knowing that the redness at sunset is a redness in vision due to the length of the red rays, which appear only at sunset when the sun is at its farthest point, so that only the red light reaches us, while the remaining lights radiate through the cosmos and do not reach us.

Therefore: the word ﴿ḍiyāʾ﴾ may be taken as the plural of ḍawʾ, like sawṭ (plural siyāṭ), ḥawḍ (plural ḥiyāḍ), and rawḍ (plural riyāḍ); or it may be taken as a singular.

The former is suitable for the general meaning, and the latter for the analytical meaning. For this reason the Truth, glory be to Him, says in another verse:

{Blessed is He who placed in the heaven constellations (burūj) and placed in it a lamp (sirāj) and a luminous moon} (25:61). The sirāj is that which gives light and heat, and it is a fitting description of the sun. Here the Truth says: {He it is Who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light and determined for it stages}. The word ﴿wa-qaddarahu﴾ apparently refers to the moon. But in reality the sun also has stages (manāzil), and the Truth said ﴿wa-qaddarahu﴾ because there is a thing called "the making" (al-jaʿl). He, glory be to Him, made the sun a radiance and made the moon a light.

Therefore: the making (al-jaʿl) relates to two matters: a making for the sun, a radiance, and a making for the moon, a light. This very making Allah made so that we may measure time by it. It is suitable for both the sun and the moon, so that we may know the number of years and the reckoning.

In acts of worship we need to determine the beginning of the month of Ramadan, so that we may observe the fast; we need to determine the months of Hajj; and a woman, for example, needs to reckon the months of her ʿidda (waiting period). All these reckonings depend on the crescent (hilāl), which is a clear sign for everyone: it begins small, grows, and then diminishes. ﴿And for the moon We have determined stages until it returns like the old date-stalk (ʿarjūn)﴾ (36:39). The ʿarjūn is what we call the sabāṭa, the stalk that carries the clusters (shamārīkh) of dates; in former times they used to make from it the brooms with which they swept the houses of the desert and the countryside. Thus Allah gave us an image from the environment in which the ancient Arab lived.

At the beginning of every month we all see the crescent as a sign announcing the birth of the month. Thus man learned to reckon the months by determining the stages of the moon. As for the year, the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the Book of Allah, the day He created the heavens and the earth…﴾ (9:36). The reckoning here is twelve lunar months. As for the day, it is measured by the sun; therefore it enters into the reckoning of stages. Thus we find that the Truth, glory be to Him, willed to make "the making" apply to two matters: the made thing of the sun and the made thing of the moon, confirming His saying: ﴿and determined for it stages, that you might know the number of years and the reckoning. Allah did not create that except in truth.﴾

The Truth, as is clear, is the established thing that does not change. When we contemplate the course of the celestial spheres, the course of the sun and the course of the moon, we find no contradiction in them. Rather, we find that the observatories of the unbelievers announce the times when the moon appears between the earth and the sun, and when the earth comes between the moon and the sun, which causes the two phenomena of the solar eclipse and the lunar eclipse; and you find all these matters with them in extreme precision.

﴿Nor can the sun overtake the moon, nor does the night outpace the day, but each in an orbit floats﴾ (36:40). This wise statement affirmed for the Arabs a judgement they believed, and negated another judgement they believed. The Arabs believed that the night precedes the day, as evidenced by the fact that the determination of the first night of Ramadan is the appointed time at which the month of fasting begins; and since they judged that the night precedes the day, there must be a counter-judgement: that the day does not precede the night.

The Qur'an came to the matter on which there was agreement and left it aside, namely that the day does not precede the night as the Arabs believed, and the Qur'an negated that either the night or the day precedes the other. The addressee, then, believed that the night precedes the day, and Allah corrects the concepts: neither the night precedes the day nor the day precedes the night.

Thus the Truth, glory be to Him, presented the cosmic matters in the Qur'an in a symbolic manner; for had He come with the scientific clarification of them, the Arabs would have denied the Qur'an. Had the Qur'an stated plainly that the earth is spherical, people would have opposed that at the time of its revelation, and we still find those who oppose that fact at the end of the twentieth century. Therefore the Truth did not disclose all the cosmic realities, but pointed to them in a manner the Arab could accept.

Since the night does not precede the day, nor the day the night, how then did this come about?

We say: did Allah create the sun facing the surface of the earth first, and then the sun set and the night came? This would be valid if the earth were flat, but the Truth, glory be to Him, created the earth spherical. That is evidence that the Truth, glory be to Him, created the sun and the earth in a configuration in which night and day exist together, and this is only possible if the earth is spherical: the half facing the sun is in daytime, and the half not facing it is in night-time; then the earth rotates, so day comes to the part that was in night, and night comes to the part that was in day.

Therefore: the Truth, glory be to Him, related in the Noble Qur'an concerning cosmic matters that the minds would discover after the Qur'an's revelation, and treated them with wisdom and precision. As an example, we find His saying:

{And He it is Who made the night and the day alternating (khilfa) for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful} (25:62).

The night is succeeded (khalfa) by the day, and the meaning of khilfa is that one replaces the other. An example from our own lives is found in guard rotations: a man guards a site for six hours, for instance, and after the guard period ends he hands the duty over to a second guard, so one succeeds the other. But who began the first guard duty before the one came to take over the shift from him?

Likewise the matter with night and day: Allah, glory be to Him, made clear that night and day are alternating, meaning that each of them had existed from the beginning; and because the earth rotates, day came to the lands upon which the sun shines, and night came to the lands from which the sun is hidden, and night and day succeeded one another. Thus Allah, glory be to Him, detailed His signs for us, and He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿He details the signs for a people who know.﴾

1 Stages of the moon (manāzil al-qamar): the positions through which it moves, i.e., its orbit around the earth, and its locations between the sun and the earth; and according as these positions change, its shape as we see it changes. Allah, exalted, said: {And the moon—We have determined for it stages until it returns like the old date-stalk} (36:39), and He, glory be to Him, said: {He it is who splits the daybreak and made the night for rest and the sun and moon for reckoning} (6:96).
2 Qiwām of everything: that by which it stands, the pillar and order of a thing. From it is the saying of Allah, exalted: {And do not give the foolish your property, which Allah has made for you a means of support} (4:5), i.e., by which your livelihoods are sustained through trade and other things.
3 Furāt: water of extreme sweetness. It is said: māʾ furāt, and nahr Furāt (the Euphrates). Allah, exalted, said: {And it is He who merged the two seas, one sweet and palatable} (25:53), and said: {And not equal are the two bodies of water, one sweet and palatable, pleasant to drink} (35:12), and said: {And We placed therein firm, lofty mountains and gave you to drink sweet water} (77:27). [Al-Muʿjam al-Waṣīṭ: root f-r-t]
4 Ḍiyāʾ may be taken as singular on the basis that ḍiyāʾ is the source of the colours of nature, and may be taken on the basis of the colours emanating from ḍiyāʾ; and this is an indication of the secrets of God in His creation.
5 Among the meanings of burūj: the constellations, the stars, and mansions; and burj (pl. abrāj) of the sphere, which are twelve constellations beginning with Aries. Allah, exalted, said: {By the sky containing constellations} (85:1), and said: {And We have placed in the sky constellations} (15:16), and said: {Even if you were in towers well-built} (4:78). [Lisān al-ʿArab: root b-r-j]
6 Sirāj: the bright lamp lit at night; the sun is described as a sirāj because it is the lamp of the day, i.e., its lamp and the source of its light. Allah, exalted, said: {And We made a blazing lamp} (78:13), and said: {And made the moon therein a light and made the sun a lamp} (71:16). [Lisān al-ʿArab: root s-r-j]
7 Allah, exalted, said: {And He subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term} (13:2), and said: {And the sun runs to its stationary point; that is the decree of the Exalted in Might, the Knowing} (36:38), and said: {The sun and the moon [follow] a precise calculation} (55:5).
8 Jaʿl: to create or to make into. Allah, exalted, said: {And We made from water every living thing} (21:30), and said: {And He made them like eaten straw} (105:5), and said: {And We made your sleep a rest, and We made the night as clothing, and We made the day for livelihood} (78:9–11). [Lisān al-ʿArab: root j-ʿ-l]
9 On the authority of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The month is twenty-nine [nights]; so when you see the crescent, fast, and when you see it, break the fast; but if it is obscured from you, then estimate it." Recorded by Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ (1080).
10 The months of Hajj are: Shawwāl, Dhū al-Qaʿda, and the first ten of Dhū al-Ḥijja. Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: The months of Hajj are Shawwāl, Dhū al-Qaʿda, and ten of Dhū al-Ḥijja (Fiqh al-Sunna 1/462). It is also said the whole month of Dhū al-Ḥijja.
11 ʿIdda: derived from counting and enumeration, i.e., what the woman counts and reckons of days and menstrual periods (qurūʾ). It has types according to the woman's condition. If she is a wife not yet consummated, she has two states; if she is divorced, there is no ʿidda upon her; but if her husband dies, her ʿidda is four months and ten days. If she has been consummated, then either she is one who menstruates, so her ʿidda is three qurūʾ, or she is one who does not menstruate, so her ʿidda is three months. The ʿidda of a pregnant woman is the delivery of the child, whether she is divorced or widowed. See the detailed treatment in Fiqh al-Sunna by Sayyid Sabiq (2/341, 350).
12 ʿArjūn: the dry strand or dry branch of a date cluster. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the ʿarjūn is the base of the ʿidhq, which is the cluster of fresh dates when it has aged, dried and bent. At the end of the month the moon is small and resembles the ʿarjūn. [Lisān al-ʿArab: root ʿ-r-j-n]
13 Meant by sabāṭa: the dry palm fronds.
14 Falak: the orbit of the stars; the falak of everything is its circuit and its main body. Allah, exalted, said: {Each in an orbit floats} (21:33). [Lisān al-ʿArab: root f-l-k]
15 Faṣala from a place, in the pattern ḍaraba: passed beyond it. Allah, exalted, said: {And when the caravan departed} (12:94). Fiṣāl means weaning; Allah, exalted, said: {And his weaning is in two years} (31:14). Faṣl means distinction; Yawm al-Faṣl is the Day of Resurrection; faṣl al-khiṭāb is the correct speech that distinguishes truth from falsehood. Allah, exalted, said: {Indeed, the Day of Judgement is an appointed time} (78:17). Faṣṣala a thing means to make it distinct sections; Allah, exalted, said: {And every matter We have detailed in detail} (17:12), and said: {Verses explained in detail} (7:133), i.e., clarified. From it is Allah's saying: {He details the signs for a people who know} (10:5). [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, pp. 82–83]

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 10, verse 6:

Then He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Indeed, in the alternation of the night and the day, and in what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth, there are signs for a people who are mindful of Allah.﴾ (6)

Thus the Truth has made clear the alternation of night from day, which confirms that they came into being together. He then joined to them ﴿and what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth﴾, because He, glory be to Him, created the universe with what it contains of the foundations of life: food, drink, air, and other things. Then He subjected the whole universe to serve the master, who is man.

If you look at the foundations of life, you will find in them essential needs represented in breath and air, drink and water, and food. These are the most important needs of man among the foundations of life. A person can endure hunger longer than thirst, and endure thirst longer than he can endure the lack of air; indeed, a person has no power to endure the lack of air for even the span of one inhalation and exhalation.

For this reason, the Truth willed that some people should own the food of others, because the body can endure hunger for a period that may reach a month, relying in that on the melting of the fat accumulated within it, unlike the machines that man has invented: a car cannot move even one meter without fuel. As for the body, it bears [hunger], perhaps the one who owns the food will ease the restrictions, or perhaps the hungry person will find a way to obtain what sustains him.

As for water, the Truth willed to reduce men's monopoly over it, because man has a greater need for water than for food.

As for air, glory be to Him and exalted be He, He did not make air the property of anyone, because air is the essential element of life; for this reason the word *nafs* (breath/soul/self) is derived from it: *nafs*, *nafas*, *nafs*.

If you look at air within all existence, you will find it is the means of preserving all existence: the stability of the earth and the stability of the buildings upon it, the stability of the towers, and the stability of the mountains; all of that is by the action of air, because its currents that surround all sides of things are what keep them firm, and if the air becomes rarefied in any direction around those buildings and mountains, they collapse at once.

Thus: air is what maintains balance throughout the whole universe. That is why we said: if you survey the words of the Qur'an, you will find that when the Truth, glory be to Him, speaks of the *taṣrīf*(1) of the winds, He speaks with the precision of a Creator, with the precision of a wise God. He sends down of the winds that which contains mercy, such as His saying: ﴿And We send the winds as fertilizers....﴾ (22) (al-Hijr). But when He mentions a wind, it carries punishment, such as His saying: ﴿With a furious, violent wind﴾ (6) (al-Haqqah), and such as His saying: ﴿So when they saw it as a cloud spreading over their valleys, they said, "This is a cloud bringing us rain." Rather, it is that which you were hastening — a wind wherein is a painful punishment (24), destroying everything by the command of its Lord...﴾ (25) (al-Ahqaf). Because the winds come from every direction, and so they balance the creatures, whereas the [destructive] wind comes from one direction and so overwhelms what is in its path.

Here He says: ﴿and what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: He brought the other created things in summary after having mentioned the sun and the moon as two distinct signs. Then He mentioned the heavens and the earth and the other signs within them: thunder, lightning, clouds, stars, and the elements of the universe. All of that is summarized in His saying: ﴿and what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth﴾, because if He had willed to detail them, He would have mentioned many signs and blessings, and He is the One who says: ﴿And if you tried to count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate them...﴾ (34) (Ibrahim).

The Qur'an is not a book for elaborating all matters; rather it is a book of guidance. And it is remarkable that He used "in" (inna), which conveys doubt, in His saying: ﴿And if you count the favor of Allah, you cannot enumerate it﴾, because no one, however much knowledge he is given, is able to count the blessings of Allah in the universe; and because undertaking to count implies the possibility of enumeration, and there is no possibility of such enumeration. Therefore He did not use "idha" (when), but used "in" (if), which is in the position of doubt.

Even more remarkable: you find that counting implies repetition, and Allah, glory be to Him, did not say, "If you count the blessings of Allah," but used one "blessing" (ni'mah), and if you investigate what is in one blessing, you will find in it thousands of blessings that cannot be counted.

The Truth concludes the verse with His saying: ﴿for signs for a people who are mindful of Allah.﴾ The word *ayat* (signs) is used in three senses. The first sense: the verses of the Qur'an. The second sense: the miracle that indicates the truthfulness of the Messenger(2). The third sense: that the sign bears one of the wonders of the universe that is manifest in existence, indicating the greatness of Allah, glory be to Him.

These signs were created by Allah so that they would draw attention to the Maker of these signs, and attention to the Maker of these signs is necessary so that man grows up in harmony with the universe for which he was created, such that nothing afterward comes to disturb this harmony. Suppose a person was at ease in his worldly life and then encountered the Hereafter in misery and hellfire: what benefit did he gain from that?

Thus: every matter that ends in extinction cannot be considered a lasting blessing, because a blessing means that you enjoy it with an enjoyment that gives you certainty that it will not leave you and you will not leave it; and the world is shorter than its inhabitants' lives. Either the blessing escapes the person in it, or he escapes the blessing.

The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted be He, keeps those who wish to be mindful of Allah, so that they may reach a bliss that does not pass away and is not taken away; and they must reflect upon the signs of the universe, because when they look at the signs of the universe with deep contemplation, they have gained two benefits. The first benefit: that they benefit from what Allah created. The second benefit: that they take a lesson from the fact that this universe which Allah created was made by Him only as a means and a passage to something else. He created creatures in it so they would live by means (asbab), but He wants to hand them over afterward to a life in which they live by the one who causes (musabbib), who is Allah. Those who are mindful are those who turn their attention, and those who are not mindful do not take heed by reflecting on the universe; things pass by man and they do not take them as lessons, as Allah said:

﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth they pass by while they turn away from it.﴾ (105) (Yusuf).

Thus: they do not turn their attention to what is in the signs of the Truth that indicate the greatness of the power of Allah, glory be to Him; they are not keen to protect themselves from the punishment of the Hereafter.

(1) *Taṣrīf al-riyāḥ* is turning them from one direction to another; *taṣrīf al-umūr* is managing them from one state to another. *Al-ṣarf* is returning a thing from one state to another. *Ṣarf al-nuqūd* is changing or spending them; *ṣarf al-sajīn* is releasing the prisoner; *ṣarf al-qulūb* is turning them from guidance to misguidance, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah turned their hearts away﴾ (127) (al-Tawbah). Al-Qamus al-Qawim vol. 1, pp. 74–75.

(2) Ibn al-Sikkit and al-Azhari said: *lawāqiḥ* means "carrying," because the winds carry water and clouds, turn them and direct them, then milk them. He the Exalted said: ﴿And He it is who sends the winds as heralds before His mercy, until when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land, and We send down water therewith and bring forth with it all kinds of fruits﴾ (57) (al-A'raf). (Lisan al-'Arab, root l-q-ḥ, adapted.)

(3) *Ṣirr* and *ṣarṣar*: extremely cold and loud wind. He the Exalted said: ﴿like a wind wherein is a cold blast﴾ (117) (Al 'Imran). (Lisan al-'Arab, root ṣ-r-r.) ['Atiyah]: extremely strong. *Al-'Ati* is the tyrant. (Lisan al-'Arab, root '-t-w.)

(4) *Al-'arid*: a cloud when it is in one part of the sky, and the 'arid is white in color. (Lisan al-'Arab, root '-r-ḍ.)

(5) *Tadham*: attacks violently until it covers what is in its path. (Lisan al-'Arab, root d-h-m, adapted.)

(6) The *ayah* in the sense of a miracle indicating the truthfulness of the Messenger, which the Qur'an reports on the tongues of the polytheists and disbelievers. He the Exalted said: ﴿And those who do not know say, "Why does Allah not speak to us or a sign come to us?"﴾ (118) (al-Baqarah), and like their saying: ﴿And they say, "Why was a sign not sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Indeed, Allah is able to send down a sign, but most of them do not know."﴾ (37) (al-An'am).

(7) These are the signs indicating Allah's power to create and to direct and arrange the universe in an order beyond imagination, such as His saying: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and the diversity of your languages and colors. Indeed, in that are signs for those of knowledge (22). And among His signs is your sleep by night and by day and your seeking of His bounty. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who hear (23). And among His signs He shows you lightning, producing fear and hope, and sends down water from the sky by which He gives life to the earth after its death. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who reason (24).﴾ (al-Rum).

(8) Attention to the Maker requires three stages: the stage of perception, the stage of emotion, and the stage of choice. Perceiving the sign makes you be moved by it; when you are moved, you choose the Maker in monotheism with love and worship, with purity and harmony with good character, and here blessings are completed by the company of Allah.

(9) *A'rada yu'ridu i'rāḍan*, so he is *mu'rid*; the plural is *mu'ridūn*. *A'rada 'an al-shay'*: when he turns his back on a thing and moves away from it. (Lisan al-'Arab, root '-r-ḍ, adapted.)

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 10 (Yunus), verse 7:

Then the Truth says, after that:

﴿Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us, and are content with the worldly life and at rest in it, and those who are heedless of Our signs (7).﴾

Al-raja' (hope, expectation) is seeking a beloved thing that is anticipated as possible. Al-tamanni (wishing) is seeking a beloved thing that cannot occur. Yet by your wish you declare that it is something you love, like the one who said: "Would that youth would return one day, so that old age might tell it what it has done." By this saying he shows that youth is a beloved and desired thing. But can this happen? Certainly not. So wishing is seeking a beloved thing that cannot happen. Likewise the poet's words: "Would that the stars would come close to me so that I could string them, a necklace of praise; I would not be pleased with my speech for you."

This is not possible.

As for hope, it is seeking a beloved thing that may happen.

Here the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿those who do not expect to meet Us﴾. Why do they not expect to meet God? Because the one who expects to meet God is the one who has prepared himself for that meeting, so that he may receive God's reward. But the one who has not done the things that qualify him for God's reward, and has done the things that qualify him for God's punishment, how can he expect to meet God? He does not expect it.(1)

For example, a man who seeks martyrdom and offers himself for it, while his self is the dearest thing to him, does so only because he is certain that what he will receive through martyrdom is better than what he leaves behind in life.

So the one who expects to meet God is the one who prepares himself for that meeting: he fears God in His commands and fears God in His prohibitions. For this reason, various events pass over a person, and in the measure of certainty they are between two things: good deeds and bad deeds. Each person knows which good deeds he has done and which bad deeds he has committed, and no one deceives himself. If he is alive, hope may lead him to deny himself, and he sees only the enticements he has missed.

But when the moment of the death rattle(2) comes, he reviews his whole record. If it was good, his face brightens; if it was bad, his face darkens. For this reason it is said: "So-and-so's end was bad," and "So-and-so's end was radiant." This is a correct saying, because at the moment the soul is seized, it leaves the body in the state it is in at the moment of parting. If he was laughing and joyful, he has seen some of the good that awaits him.

A person at the time of the death rattle does not lie to himself. When he falls ill, he hopes for recovery; but when the time of the end of life arrives, his deeds are displayed to him rapidly. If the deeds are good, his features relax, because he anticipates the reward he will meet.

This is like a student who has been diligent and industrious, and then they tell him, "Someone has brought you the result," and he goes to it calmly. But if he has not been diligent and has not prepared, he fears meeting the one who carries the result.

So too, those who expect to meet God have worked in preparation for that meeting and await their reward from God. But those who have not worked fear meeting God and do not hope for it, and the reason is that they have not worked for the Hereafter. ﴿and are content with the worldly life and at rest in it﴾, as though they have been satisfied with it and have not desired the Hereafter. God has named this abode with a name that, as soon as we hear it, should turn us away from it, so He said: ﴿the worldly life﴾. There is no name lower than this, while the opposite of the worldly life is the higher life.(3)

A person may study the age of this world and say: it will last ten million years, or a hundred million years, and yet not notice that his own lifespan is the appointed term of this world.

So, for you, the world is the measure of your lifespan within it, not its actual lifespan until the Hour arrives. And what benefit do you gain from it if it lasts for others? For a person, the age of the world is the length of his stay in it, which is a guess and not a certainty. He may die in his mother's womb, or die at a month old, or a year old, or after reaching a hundred. So the one who is content with what is uncertain is short-sighted.

For this reason, look at the Qur'an when it says: ﴿Are you content with the worldly life instead of the Hereafter? But the enjoyment(4) of the worldly life, compared with the Hereafter, is only a little.﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:38).

Even if you measure the age of the world from the beginning of creation until the Hour arrives, it is still heading to annihilation. As long as it is heading to annihilation, it is a little enjoyment. Whoever is at rest with this little enjoyment is heedless. Therefore the Truth ends the verse with: ﴿and those who are heedless of Our signs﴾, the reverse of what He said about those who know the value of work for the Hereafter.

When the Truth says: ﴿Indeed there are signs for a people who fear God﴾ (Yunus 10:6), heedlessness (al-ghaflah)(5) is the departure of meaning from the self. As long as meaning exists in the self, wakefulness exists and heedlessness departs. So heedlessness is the departure of meaning from the self, and wakefulness is the settling of meaning in the self.

We know that the information which the human mind receives is captured by the focal point of consciousness (bu'rat al-shu'ur)(6), just as a photographic camera captures any image.

Beware of thinking that a person knows information by repeating it twice or more, because all minds agree that they capture information from a single time. What distinguishes one person from another is his ability to receive information with a mind prepared for it, because the focal point of consciousness captures only one meaning. Then that meaning shifts to the margin of consciousness to make room for the second piece of information. If information is received while another meaning is in the focal point of your consciousness, the information does not settle. For this reason you repeat the reading once, twice, three times, until the information finds the focal point of consciousness empty.

An example of this is a student trying to memorize a poem: if his mind is prepared to receive the poem, he memorizes it in one go.

So the mind is like a photographic apparatus. For this reason the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, says: ﴿God has not made for any man two hearts within his body...﴾ (al-Ahzab 33:4).

If you want to receive some information, be keen to empty your mind of any other information, so that the new information meets an empty focal point of consciousness and settles in it.

A successful teacher is one who draws the minds of all his students to what he says, and as long as their minds are turned to him, not a word passes without the students absorbing it. This is the opposite of an unsuccessful teacher who performs his work with monotony(8) and weakness(9) that turns the students away from him. And we find that the successful teacher, when he draws his students' attention, pauses the lesson to ask any one of them about what he said, and the students then listen attentively, because each of them expects to be asked about the information that was just given.

The diligent student is the one who reads the lesson with a mind able to discuss its styles and information, and he keeps his presence of mind while reading. But the failing student reads without alertness or attention.

Another example: a farmer who sleeps at the edge of the well of the water-wheel does not fall into it, because he sleeps while keeping in mind that if he turns onto his side he will fall into the well.(10) Likewise, when two brothers sleep on one bed, each gets up in the morning keeping in mind that there is another beside him. But if each of them sleeps in a separate bed, he wakes to find his head in one direction and his legs in another. This process is called retention and wakefulness, and one says: "So-and-so is alert" (yaqizh), and the word yaqizh is the opposite of "asleep" (na'im),(11) because the one who is awake retains awareness and attention.

So heedlessness is the departure of meaning from the self and its effacement. Those who pass by the signs while heedless of them will gain nothing from these signs, and then the outcome of their heedlessness comes to them in the Hereafter.

The Truth, glory be to Him, says about them: ﴿Those—their abode is the Fire, because of what they used to earn (8).﴾

(1) Al-raja': hope expected to be near; the opposite of despair. One says "rajahu, yarjuhu, rajwan and rija'" when he expects it with desire for it and joy in it, or with fear of it. Raja' is also used in the sense of fear. God, exalted, said: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not expect dignity from God? (13)﴾ (Nuh 71:13). And His words: ﴿Indeed those who do not expect to meet Us...(7)﴾ (Yunus 10:7), meaning: those who do not fear meeting Us or do not hope for Our continuance, and so they do not prepare their souls for this great meeting with righteous deeds. Al-rija' also means a side; its plural is arja'. God said: ﴿and the angels will be on its sides (17)﴾ (al-Haqqah 69:17).

(2) Al-ghargharah: the rattling of the soul in the throat (Lisan al-'Arab, root gh-r-r). The moments of the death rattle, when the soul reaches the throat, are the point at which the acceptance of repentance ends. On the authority of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "God accepts the repentance of His servant as long as he has not reached the death rattle." Recorded by Ahmad in his Musnad (2/132), al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (3537), who said: a hasan gharib hadith; al-Hakim in his Mustadrak (4/257), who authenticated it, and al-Dhahabi agreed; and Ibn Hibban (2449, Mawarid al-Zam'an).

(3) On the authority of al-Mustawrid ibn Shaddad, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "By God, the world compared with the Hereafter is only like one of you dipping his finger into the sea; let him see what it returns with." Recorded by Muslim in his Sahih (2858), Ahmad in his Musnad (4/229, 230), and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (2323), who said: a hasan sahih hadith.

(4) God mentions al-mata', al-istimta' and al-tamtii' in several places in His Book. Although their meanings differ, they go back to one root. Al-mata' is everything that is benefited from, provides sustenance and is taken as provision, and it is subject to annihilation in this world. God said: ﴿Say: The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for one who fears God (77)﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:77). He said: ﴿Repent to Him, and He will grant you a good enjoyment until an appointed term (3)﴾ (Hud 11:3). He said: ﴿He said: God forbid that we take anyone except him with whom we found our property (79)﴾ (Yusuf 12:79). He said: ﴿And when they opened their goods, they found their merchandise returned to them. They said: O our father, what more could we want? This is our merchandise, returned to us (65)﴾ (Yusuf 12:65). He said: ﴿Those who disbelieve wish that you would be heedless of your weapons and your goods (102)﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:102). He said: ﴿Whoever enjoys the 'umrah until the Hajj (196)﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:196). (Lisan al-'Arab, root m-t-', adapted.)

(5) Aghfaltu al-shay': I left the thing neglected while you were mindful of it. God said: ﴿and they were heedless of them (136)﴾ (al-A'raf 7:136), meaning: in their abandonment of faith in God and of reflection upon Him, they were in the position of the heedless, or they were heedless of the reward that would be given for it (Lisan al-'Arab, root gh-f-l).

(6) Bu'rat al-shu'ur: the centres of feeling, sensation and perception in the brain. The bu'rah of anything is its centre (al-Mu'jam al-Wasit, root b-'-r, adapted).

(7) It refers to the thinking heart, and the Qur'an often uses it in the sense of intellect, as in God's words: ﴿Do they not reflect on the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts? (24)﴾ (Muhammad 47:24), and He said: ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand (179)﴾ (al-A'raf 7:179), meaning: minds. The heart rejects duality in thought, and from here the focal point of consciousness is formed in the one who speaks, the existing one, and the single thought.

(8) Al-ratabah: moving or following one fixed system that does not change (Lisan al-'Arab, root r-t-b).

(9) Al-rakakah: weakness in wording and style.

(10) The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade sleeping on the roof of a house that has no hijar, that is, a parapet preventing one from falling from the roof. On the authority of 'Ali ibn Shayban, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sleeps on a roof that has no hijar, the protection of God is removed from him." Recorded by Abu Dawud in his Sunan (5041), and similar in Ahmad's Musnad (5/79, 271).

(11) Al-yaqzah: the opposite of sleep. It may also be the opposite of heedlessness and lack of perceptiveness. One says: "a man is yaqiz and yaqiz" when he is alert, with knowledge and discernment.

And you say, "I took refuge in such-and-such" (1), when it is the place that protects you from something (2). Here the Truth says: ﴿Their refuge is the Fire.﴾ So if that is the refuge, then necessarily whatever is outside it will be, for them, a greater punishment. They take refuge in the Fire ﴿because of what they used to earn﴾, i.e., because of the sins and misdeeds they used to commit.

(1) Awaytu: I sought refuge. Al-ma'wa is a noun of place (on the pattern maf'al) from awa, ya'wi, and al-ma'wa means dwelling and place. That is, their place, their abode and their settling will be in the Fire, in return for what they did of sin and wrongdoing and their heedlessness of the Truth and its clear signs (Lisan al-'Arab, root a-w-a, with adaptation...).

(2) An example of this is the saying of Nuh (peace be upon him) when the flood covered the earth: ﴿I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾ (Hud 11:43).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 10, verse 9:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds – their Lord guides them by their faith. Rivers will flow beneath them in Gardens of Bliss.﴾ (9)

Here the Truth, glorified is He, speaks of the counterpart, namely those who believe, and informs us that He, glorified is He: ﴿their Lord guides them by their faith﴾.

Guidance (hidayah) – as we said before – means pointing to what is good, by the method that the Truth, glorified is He, sent to us, and through which the Truth made the paths clear before the believer and the disbeliever. As for the one who turns to Allah in faith, the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, gives him another guidance: He lightens the burdens of obedience upon him, and increases him in guidance by what is known. Therefore He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is difficult except for the humble (khashi'in)(1)﴾ (al-Baqarah, 45).

Thus the believer receives the requirements of obedience with love; so the Truth, glorified is He, makes them easy for him and causes him to perceive the pleasure of this obedience, so that its hardship becomes light for him, and He, glorified is He, also supports him with help.

The Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds – their Lord guides them by their faith(2)﴾. Since they have believed, He, glorified is He, sends down for them the rulings that benefit them in their lives and profit them in their Hereafter; or guidance is not only in this world but in the Hereafter. So, since they have believed, they have taken the method from Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and performed righteous deeds, and the Truth, glorified is He, guides them to the path of Paradise.

For this reason the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿On the day you see the believing men and believing women, their light running before them and at their right hands… (12)﴾ (al-Hadid), and He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And those who believed with him – their light runs before them and at their right hands; they say, "Our Lord, perfect for us our light…" (8)﴾ (al-Tahrim). That is: their light illuminates before them. As for the hypocrites, they say to those who believed: ﴿Wait for us that we may acquire (naqtabis)(3) from your light." It will be said, "Return behind you and seek (faltamisu)(4) light…" (13)﴾ (al-Hadid). That is: this is not the time for seeking light; the time for seeking light was in the world, by following the method and performing righteous deeds, as much as one can.

So: the Truth, glorified is He, guides the believers to a light above their light in the Hereafter.

The verse allows for guidance in this world, and it allows for guidance in the Hereafter.

The Truth, glorified is He, describes the condition of the believers in the Hereafter, saying: ﴿Rivers will flow beneath them in Gardens of Bliss (9)﴾ (Yunus).

We have said that Paradise is on the banks of rivers, because greenery originates from water. Wherever you see a watercourse, you must find greenery. And the "gardens" are not the houses, as evidenced by the Truth's saying: ﴿And pleasant dwellings in Gardens of Eden (adn)(5)… (72)﴾ (al-Tawbah). We find the Truth, glorified is He, saying once: ﴿Rivers flow beneath them… (100)﴾ (al-Tawbah), and He, glorified is He, says in other places(6): ﴿Rivers flow beneath them… (25)﴾ (al-Baqarah).

The Truth, glorified is He, gives us a varied image of water that does not cease; it is water self-existent in Paradise that never ends.

1 Imam Abu Hamid al-Ghazali said in his book "Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din" (1/171): "Khushu' is the fruit of faith and the result of certainty of the majesty of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Whoever is granted it will be humble in prayer, and outside prayer, and in his solitude, and in the treasury when needed. For the requirement of khushu' is knowledge of Allah, Exalted, upon the servant, knowledge of His majesty, and knowledge of the servant's shortcomings. From these knowledges khushu' is generated, and it is not restricted to prayer." The Shaykh indicates that the Qur'an is guidance, the Messenger, by his Sunnah, is its evidence, and Allah is the helper in it; and reaching companionship (ma'iyyah) is itself nearness to Allah.

2 The "bi" in ﴿bi-imanihim﴾ may carry two meanings: that it is causal, i.e., because of their faith in the world, Allah guides them on the Day of Resurrection upon the Straight Path until they cross it and bring them safely into Paradise; or that it is for assistance (isti'anah), i.e., their faith becomes a light by which they walk on the Path. See the tafsirs of al-Qurtubi (4/3238) and Ibn Kathir (2/408).

3 Naqtabis: we take. Allah the Exalted said, relating about Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it a burning brand or find at the fire guidance (10)﴾ (Ta-Ha), and He said: ﴿I will bring you from it news or bring you a burning brand that you may warm yourselves (7)﴾ (al-Naml). The qabas is the fire, and iqtibas is taking from it. The acquiring of light from the light of the people of Paradise is evidence of the intensity and strength of this light (Lisan al-'Arab, root q-b-s, with adaptation).

4 Faltamisu: seek. Iltamasa al-shay' and talamasahu: he sought it (Lisan al-'Arab, root l-m-s).

5 'Adana fulan bi-l-makan ya'dunu 'adnan wa 'udnan: he resided. The origin of everything is its ma'dan (place of origin), and Gardens of Adn: that is, gardens of lasting residence in a place of eternity. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Gardens of Eden, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever (76)﴾ (Ta-Ha).

6 The saying of the Exalted, ﴿min tahtiha al-anhar (from beneath them the rivers flow)﴾ occurs 35 times in the Qur'an, and ﴿tajri tahtaha al-anhar (rivers flow beneath it)﴾ occurs once.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 10, verse 10:

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says:

﴿Their call therein will be: "Glory be to You, O Allah," and their greeting therein will be "Peace," and the close of their call will be: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾

"Their call" means their supplication.

Is the Hereafter a abode of obligation, so that they continue worshipping Allah? No. Rather, it is a worship of delight. Whenever they see something, they say: "We have been given this before," but when they eat the fruits of Paradise they know that what is on earth resembled those fruits, yet was not like them.

﴿They will say: "This is what we were provided with before," and they will be given it in semblance...﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:25).

Or they say: ﴿Glory be to You, O Allah﴾ as an acknowledgment of the blessing. When you see something that pleases you, you say: "Glory be to You, O Lord." After the blessing comes to you and you say: "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to Allah), and you are surprised by things you had not expected, because of the excess of their beauty, you say: "Al-hamdu lillah" (Praise be to Allah).[1]

So you receive the blessing with "Subhan Allah," and you conclude the blessing with "Al-hamdu lillah." Therefore the Truthful, glorified is He, says: ﴿And the close of their call will be: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾

What makes the life of this world meaningful, gives it flavour and gives it stability, is that a person be at peace. The meaning of peace (salam) is tranquillity and contentment; there are no agitators, no disturbers, and this does not come about without the absence of collision within the faculties of the soul. Thus a person attains peace with himself, peace with his family, and this is the second circle; peace with his people, and peace with the whole world. All of that is called peace, meaning: there is no one who troubles him, neither from himself, nor from his family, nor from his people, nor from the world. The wider the scope of peace, the more a person's sense of tranquillity increases.

When the Truthful, glorified is He, says: ﴿And their greeting therein will be "Peace",﴾ peace occurs in many matters. The Truthful, glorified is He, says: ﴿Indeed, the companions of Paradise today are busy in enjoyment, they and their spouses, in shade, reclining upon couches. For them therein is fruit, and for them is whatever they request. "Peace," a word from a Lord, Merciful.﴾ (Ya-Sin 36:55–58). This is the peace that has meaning, for it is peace from Allah. He did not say, glorified is He, "a peace that bequeaths you and a soul at rest" only; rather it is peace spoken by Allah, and see what happiness it is when the Truthful, the Exalted, addresses you directly. There is a difference between Allah spreading peace upon you and His speech greeting you with peace. This is the reason for His saying: ﴿"Peace," a word from a Lord, Merciful﴾ (Ya-Sin 36:58). This is the peace of Allah. Then, after this station, comes the peace of the angels: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, [saying], "Peace be upon you..."﴾ (Al-Ra'd 13:23–24). So the Truthful's words here, ﴿And their greeting therein will be "Peace",﴾ contain the word peace, a symbol of contentment and stability in Paradise. Peace is the first sensation you love in yourself, even if all the people are against you. But when you settle, you ask yourself: "What have I done that some are against me?" And when you answer yourself: "I have only done good," you feel peace in yourself. And when others welcome what you do, life flows on, without opposition or rancour. This is what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man of the people of Paradise will appear to you now." (ﷺ)

"There entered a man whom the people recognised. When he departed, one of the Companions[2] rose and went to a man to learn what he did, and asked him: 'What do you do that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave you the glad tidings of Paradise?' He found the man's conduct upright and following the method without addition, so the Companion asked him: 'Why then did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) give you the glad tidings of Paradise?'

The man said: 'By Allah, I pray as you pray, I fast as you fast, and I give zakat as you give it, but I sleep with no rancour in my heart against anyone.'

This is inner peace. When a person reaches peace with himself, the world's turmoil does not harm him, and afterwards he is assured that his peace with Allah, the Exalted, will be present. Whoever has peace with himself, with his environment and with his society, he attains peace from Allah, glorified is He. The Qur'an tells us about those who suffer a predicament in the Hereafter: ﴿On the Day when it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission. Then among them are the wretched and the fortunate﴾ (Hud 11:105).

These are the ones who are wretched in the Fire. As for those who are fortunate in Paradise, what of the state of those who are neither wretched nor fortunate, who are the people of al-A'raf? Because on the Day of Resurrection people are divided into three categories. Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿As for one whose scales are heavy, he will be in a pleasant life. But as for one whose scales are light, his refuge will be an abyss.﴾ (Al-Qari'ah 101:6–9). Allah, the Truthful, did not tell us the matter of those whose two sides were equal during the reckoning, because He, glorified is He, said in a sacred hadith: "My mercy overcame My wrath."[3] Allah, the Truthful, shows us His mercy when He says:

﴿And the companions of Paradise will call out to the companions of the Fire: "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised to be true?" They will say, "Yes." Then a crier will announce between them: "The curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers.﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:44).

Then the matter of the men of al-A'raf comes, when He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And on the heights are men who recognise each by his mark...﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:46). They recognised the believers by their marks and recognised the disbelievers by their marks. Some of them sat on al-A'raf, waiting and looking at the people of Paradise, saying: ﴿"Peace be upon you," they have not entered it, though they aspire [to].﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:46).

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, gives us a second picture, when He says: ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of Paradise: "Pour upon us some water or from what Allah has provided you." They will say, "Indeed, Allah has forbidden them to the disbelievers."﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:50).

So the people of al-A'raf are made happy by the bounty of Allah given to the people of Paradise, and they hope that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, will forgive them.

In our life we hear the supervisors of prisoners, or of those sentenced to death, say: before a criminal is sentenced to death his weight drops, then it increases after the sentence, because the matter has settled. Those who occupy themselves with knowing their place in the Hereafter, whether it is in Paradise or in the Fire, do not forget to say to the believers: ﴿"Peace be upon you..."﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:46).

Here the Truthful, glorified is He, says of the people of Paradise: ﴿And their greeting therein will be "Peace", and the close of their call will be: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ And perhaps "the close of their call" means their last word.

Each of them says: "I praised my Lord for such-and-such a thing." The last praise is the summit of praise, because they praised Allah for the blessing in this world, which passes away, and they praise Him in the Hereafter for the blessing that does not pass away. Praise for a blessing that does not pass away is the summit of praise.[4]

1. Receiving a blessing with "Subhan Allah" is an exclamation of admiration at a beauty that leads you to tanzih (declaring Allah transcendent), tawhid (affirmation of His oneness) and tafrid (singling Him out), so you utter tawhid in beauty and majesty and tanzih. When the blessing is complete, the utterance comes spontaneously: ﴿That the praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ (Yunus 10:10). So the first is admiration with tanzih, and the last is praise with certainty.

2. Fakihun: luxuriant, delighting in the bliss of Paradise. Allah says: ﴿Jesting in what their Lord has given them﴾ (Al-Tur 52:18).

3. Al-ara'ik: the thrones or furnishings, or a bed in a canopied enclosure without a curtain; or it is anything one reclines on, such as a couch, bed or dais. Allah says: ﴿Reclining therein on couches; how excellent the reward and how good a resting place﴾ (Al-Kahf 18:31). (Lisan al-Arab, root a-r-k, adapted.)

4. The complete form of this hadith: Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) said: We were sitting with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he said: "A man of the people of Paradise will appear to you now." A man of the Ansar appeared, his beard dripping with water from his ablution, having hung his sandals in his left hand. The next day the Prophet (ﷺ) said the same, and that man appeared as he had the first time. On the third day the Prophet (ﷺ) said the same again, and that man appeared in his first state. When the Prophet (ﷺ) rose, 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As followed him and said: "I have quarrelled with my father, and I swore not to enter upon him for three days. If you see fit to shelter me with you until it passes, I will do so." He said: "Yes." Anas said: 'Abdullah used to narrate that he stayed with that man those three nights and did not see him rise at night for anything, except that whenever he turned in his bed he remembered Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and glorified Him until he rose for the dawn prayer. 'Abdullah said: "However, I never heard him say anything but good. When the three nights had passed, and I was almost belittling his deeds, I said: 'O servant of Allah, there was no anger or estrangement between me and my father, but I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say three times about you: "A man of the people of Paradise will appear to you now," and you appeared three times, so I wished to shelter with you to observe your deeds and follow them, but I did not see you doing much. What then has brought you to what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said?' He said: 'It is only what you have seen.' 'Abdullah said: When I turned to leave, he called me and said: 'It is only what you have seen, except that I find in myself no deceit towards any Muslim, and I do not envy anyone for a good that Allah has given him.' 'Abdullah said: 'This is what has brought you to that, and it is what we cannot bear.'" Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (3/166) and Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd (694).

5. He is 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, a Companion from Makkah. He used to write in the pre-Islamic period and was skilled in the Syriac language. He embraced Islam before his father. Born around 7 BH and died 65 AH. He was much devoted to worship and to fighting enemies, and was known to fight with two swords. (Al-A'lam of al-Zirikli 4/111.)

6. His saying here: ﴿with His permission﴾ qualifies His saying: ﴿On the Day when every soul will come pleading for itself...﴾ (Al-Nahl 16:111). No soul may speak or plead for itself except by Allah's permission. This is not contradicted by His saying: ﴿This is a Day when they will not speak, and they will not be permitted to offer excuses﴾ (Al-Mursalat 77:35–36), because the Day of Resurrection has stations: in some of them they are not permitted to speak, so they refrain, and in others they are permitted, so they speak. (Said by Abu Yahya al-Ansari in his book Fath al-Rahman bi-Kashf ma Yaltabis fi al-Qur'an, pp. 193–194.)

7. "Their scales were heavy" means their good deeds outweighed their bad deeds. "In a pleasant life" means in Paradise; if the life is pleasing, its livelihood is one with which He is pleased. "Their scales were light" means their bad deeds outweighed their good deeds. "His refuge will be an abyss" means he will fall headfirst into the Fire of Hell; the expression "his mother" refers to his head, that is, his brain.

8. Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (3194) and Muslim in his Sahih (2751). Its complete form: from Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah had created the creation, He wrote in His book, which is with Him above the Throne: 'My mercy has overcome My wrath.'" In some narrations of the hadith the wording is: "outweighs" or "has preceded."

9. Al-A'raf in the language is the plural of 'urf, which is every high elevation. Al-Zajjaj said: al-A'raf are the high parts of a wall. Al-A'raf are the high parts of a wall between the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire. It was said concerning the people of al-A'raf that they are a group whose good deeds and bad deeds were equal, so they did not deserve Paradise by their good deeds, nor the Fire by their bad deeds, and so they were on the barrier between Paradise and the Fire. (Lisan al-Arab, root '-r-f, adapted.)

10. Al-simah: the mark by which good and evil are recognised. From it is His saying: ﴿Their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration﴾ (Al-Fath 48:29), and His saying: ﴿You recognise them by their mark; they do not ask people persistently﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:273). This is about the people of goodness and virtue. As for the wicked, Allah says of them: ﴿The criminals will be recognised by their marks, and they will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾ (Al-Rahman 55:41).

11. Praise for bringing into existence, praise for sustenance in this world, and praise for the blessing of remaining in the abode of eternity, which is the summit of praise.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (*Tafsir al-Sha'rawi*, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 10, verse 11:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:
﴿Had Allah hastened for people the evil as they hasten for the good, their term would have been decreed for them. But We leave those who do not expect the meeting with Us to wander blindly in their transgression.(1) (10:11)﴾(2)

This verse deals with a doctrinal matter that may preoccupy people in their supplication to Allah, the Exalted. Their supplication may not be answered despite its frequency, which saddens them about themselves. One of them says: "Why does Allah not accept my supplication?" Or some of them fall into despair.

We say to every person from this group: No. You supplicate. Sometimes you supplicate for evil and sometimes for good. Had Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, answered you in all your supplications, He would answer your supplication for evil and your supplication for good. And had Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, hastened for you the answer to your supplication for evil, as you would like Him to hasten for you the answer to your supplication for good, your term would have been decreed for you and the matter would have ended. Some people have said:(3) ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment.(32) (8:32)﴾ (al-Anfal). Had the Truth answered such a supplication, it would have been a calamity upon those who made that supplication.

Therefore, it is in your interest, when you supplicate against yourself(4) or supplicate for any calamity, that Allah, the Exalted, not answer you. Understand that Allah, the Exalted, has wisdom in answering, because He, glory be to Him, is exalted above being a functionary of the creation. Whoever calls upon Him for something, He must grant it to him. His will, glory be to Him, must be involved in determining the form of the answer, for if the matter were the reverse of that, divinity would have passed to the servant.

Allah, glory be to Him, has protected His servants by placing a watch over supplication. You believe that your supplication is for good, but the watch of the Truth, glory be to Him, who knows everything from eternity(5), almost says to you: No, it is not good. So await the good in the non-answering of your supplication, for He, glory be to Him, is the one who said: ﴿It may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you; and it may be that you love a thing and it is bad for you...(216) (2:216)﴾ (al-Baqarah).

Therefore, your knowledge is not final in determining good and evil. So leave the Supreme God, who is trustworthy over you, to answer or not answer what you call upon Him for, while you think it is good. The supreme knowledge is what distinguishes good from evil. Withholding is, at times, the very essence of giving.(6) Therefore the Truth says: ﴿And man prays for evil as he prays for good, and man is ever hasty.(11) (17:11)﴾ (al-Isra').

You may insist on a supplication which, if it were answered for you, would be evil. Allah, glory be to Him, knows what is good for you. Sometimes He answers some of His creatures concerning things which a person among them wished to exist, and then the person discovers that they were not good. And sometimes He brings you things you thought were evil for you, and you find good in them. Thus the Truth, glory be to Him, corrects your voluntary actions by His wisdom.

The disbelievers said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment.(32) (8:32)﴾ (al-Anfal).

Those who said this were: al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, and al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth. They had reached the peak of confusion. First, they were confused when they accused him of being a sorcerer, and they did not notice the stupidity of what they said, because if the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had the power of sorcerers, why did he not bewitch them too, so that they would also believe?

They were confused a second time, trying to say that the Qur'an is poetry (sa'r), or that it has the nature of poetry and rhymed prose (saj'), and the Qur'an is not like that. Had another group said such a statement, they would have had an excuse, because they were not people of language. But these were a people skilled in eloquence and rhetoric, who knew the markets of poetry and oratory. Then they were confused a third time, and they tried to disparage the status of Muhammad (ﷺ), while acknowledging the greatness of the Qur'an. They said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two towns?(31) (43:31)﴾ (al-Zukhruf).

When the Truth, glory be to Him, addresses an incident that occurred during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) with the disbelievers, He does not confine the event to what happened. Rather, He addresses a general universal matter, namely the establishment of the Hour, and makes the incident that occurred in His time merely a cause, so as to give the ruling a universal application in every time and every place. Otherwise, the matter would be limited to treating an event that happened to a particular person, with the ruling pertaining only to the people who were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Qur'an came to all people and came for all times. Therefore, any well-known matter, whatever it is, must be before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from people who lived with him, and it has a particular cause. But the lesson lies in the generality of the subject, not in the particularity of the cause.

In this personal matter concerning those who said that, Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, addresses a universal matter that will remain until the Hour is established.

They supplicated against themselves: ﴿If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment.(32) (8:32)﴾ (al-A'raf). As 'Ad said to Hud: ﴿Have you come to us that we should worship Allah alone and leave what our fathers used to worship? Then bring us what you threaten us with, if you are of the truthful.(70) (7:70)﴾ (al-A'raf). Therefore, they supplicated for evil against themselves.

Allah addresses the matter of supplicating for good or supplicating for evil, because a person may become distressed by matters surrounding his self or his environment. When he becomes distressed by matters surrounding him in himself, such as an illness for example, or a disability he cannot bear patiently or cannot endure, he says: "O Lord, relieve me, O Lord," and here he is supplicating against himself for death. Had Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, answered his supplication, the matter would have been settled.

But Allah is the Wise, the Mighty, who does not take orders from any of His creatures, and does not hasten at the haste of the servants. Just as He delays the answer to your supplication for good, He also delays answering your supplication for evil against yourself. In that is mercy from Him, glory be to Him.

If you say: "I supplicate for good, and Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, does not give me," then take its counterpart: you supplicate for evil against yourself, and Allah does not answer you. Does a father not sometimes become distressed with those around him and say: "Let Allah take me, so that I may rest from your faces"? Suppose that Allah, glory be to Him, responded to this supplication. What would the situation be? You may find someone who says: "O Lord, afflict me with blindness so that I do not see them," or a woman supplicates against herself or her children.

You want Allah, the Exalted, to answer your supplication, but if He answered your supplications for evil, your lives would end in terror, like this mother who supplicates with the proximate things, saying to her child, for example: "May God give me your fire to drink," thus asking to be given drink with fire, although drink is for quenching thirst and fire is for heat.

Therefore, a person may become distressed with himself, or become distressed with those around him, and so he supplicates against himself for evil. When a person supplicates, he must exalt the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, above executing what the servant supplicates for without that supplication passing through His wisdom, glory be to Him and exalted.

﴿And had Allah hastened for people the evil as they hasten for the good, their term would have been decreed for them.﴾ So whenever you accept that Allah, the Exalted, delays for you your supplications for evil against yourselves, then accept from Him the delay of your supplications for good, because the good in what you seek is other than the good in what Allah knows. He is the All-Knowing, the All-Aware. You may seek a good which you know, while Allah knows in it an evil. So it is in your interest that He not answer you. Just as you respect His non-answering in evil itself, or against one you love, respect His non-answering of you in what you think is good for you, or for one you love, because Allah does not hasten at the haste of His servants, for He is the one who created them, and He knows them best. He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Man was created of haste.(37) (21:37)﴾ (al-Anbiya'), and He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿I will show you My signs, so do not seek to hasten them.(37) (21:37)﴾ (al-Anbiya'). And if the Truth, glory be to Him, had answered those who said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones...(32) (8:32)﴾ (al-Anfal), their end would have been of the same kind as what they supplicated for, and they would have been destroyed, and then they would have ended up in the punishment of Hell.

And since the Truth, glory be to Him, willed for them to remain, so that whoever chooses faith may believe, and whoever chooses disbelief must bear the consequence of transgression. This is manifest in that each of them not only chooses disbelief, but exceeds the limit and asks those who believed to renounce their faith. In that is an overstepping of bounds. Therefore they wander blindly in this transgression, meaning that circumstances accumulate upon them, and it becomes established, for them and for those who come after them, that disbelief is powerless to confront the power of the Truth.

In life there are examples, and to Allah belongs the highest example. There is one who has his enemy in his power, so he strikes him, but does not kill him. Then the enemy repeats the offense, so he strikes him again, then the offense is repeated and he strikes him, while he never kills him, in order to continue humiliating him. The strong does not kill his opponent, but hurts him, so the opponent never lifts his head.

The Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿So We leave those who do not expect the meeting with Us to wander blindly in their transgression.﴾ That is: the Truth, glory be to Him, leaves the people of falsehood, so that their evil deeds accumulate upon them, and they taste the calamity of the enmity of Islam, so they do not raise their heads. For the people of Islam return the offense to them multiplied. The people of falsehood will surely despair that they will triumph over the truth in any way or form. Whatever they devise in methods of harming Islam, you will find that the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, grants victory to the Muslims.

The example before us is from his biography, when the Truth, glory be to Him, commanded him to emigrate, and the disbelievers were besieging his house with young men from the tribes. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out without them noticing, and he (ﷺ) said: "May their faces be disfigured."(15)

Allah willed this, so that they would know that they could not triumph over Muhammad (ﷺ), neither by direct confrontation nor by plotting deception.
