He said: "Dismount from it, and do not accompany us with one who is cursed, and do not supplicate against yourselves, do not supplicate against your children, do not supplicate against your wealth, and do not coincide with an hour from Allah in which He is asked for a gift and He responds to you." Narrated by Muslim (3009).
10 Al-wa'z: advice to obedience and righteous deeds, guidance to good. Ibn Sayyid said: it is your reminding a person of what softens his heart, of reward and punishment. [Mentioned by Ibn Manzur in Lisan, root w-'-z]. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (4/3366) regarding ﴿I advise you...﴾ (46) [Hud]: i.e., I forbid you from this question and warn you lest you be among the ignorant, i.e., the sinners. Ibn al-'Arabi said: this is an addition from Allah and an admonition by which He elevates Nuh above the station of the ignorant.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 10, verse 90:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and Pharaoh and his hosts followed them in insolence and enmity, until, when drowning overtook him, he said: "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am among the Muslims." (90)﴾

The Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea... (90)﴾: Because the crossing did not happen through human means, but through an act that goes beyond human causes. Had Musa, peace be upon him, dug a tunnel beneath the water, or had he and his people boarded ships, they would have had a share in crossing the sea. But the crossing happened through causes that are not perceptible to human beings. The Truth, glory be to Him, is the One who revealed to Musa: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff... (63)﴾ [al-Shu'ara']. The water of the sea, like any other water, is subject to the law of fluidity, and "al-istitrad" (communicating vessels, the principle by which liquid levels equalize) is the means of fluidity, which is the opposite of freezing, which is characterized by rigidity.

It is upon al-istitrad that the methods of conveying water are built: water is pumped into water tanks, which are usually higher than the height of any house, and then the water is distributed to the houses according to the theory of communicating vessels (al-awani al-mustatriqa). If there is a building taller than the tank, the residents of the building install a pump to raise the water to the upper floors.

If the law of the sea is fluidity and communicating levels, how is this communication cut off?

The Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿... so each separate part was like a huge mountain (63)﴾ [al-Shu'ara'].

So how did the water turn into mountains separated by tunnels and paths along which Musa and his people walked?

How did Musa and his people walk in tranquillity?

It must be the companionship of Allah, glory be to Him, which protects him, and it is the explanation of the words of the Truth, glory be to Him: ﴿... Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me (62)﴾ [al-Shu'ara'].

Despite this, Pharaoh and his hosts followed them, hoping to overtake them. As soon as Sayyidina Musa, peace be upon him, had succeeded in crossing with his people, he wished to strike the sea with his staff so that it would return to the law of fluidity. Had he done so, he would not have allowed Pharaoh and his hosts to walk through the passages between the waters that had turned into mountains. But Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, willed otherwise, for the Truth, glory be to Him, willed to save and to destroy by one and the same thing. So He revealed to Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And leave the sea calm (rahwan); indeed, they are an army to be drowned (24)﴾ [al-Dukhan]. That is: leave the sea in its state, so that Pharaoh and his hosts are deceived. As soon as the last soldier of them descends into the passage between the mountains of water, the sea will return to its state of fluidity, and Pharaoh and his hosts will drown, while Musa and his people are saved.

The Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Then Pharaoh and his hosts followed them... (90)﴾ [Yunus]. So was this following a sign of intent to do evil?

Could it have been Pharaoh's intention that he invite Musa and his people to return to Egypt to settle there?

No, this was not Pharaoh's intention; therefore the Truth, glory be to Him, said of this following: ﴿in insolence and enmity... (90)﴾ [Yunus]. That is: it was a following driven by desire for revenge, humiliation and aggression.

The noble Qur'an depicts the moment of Pharaoh's drowning with His words: ﴿until, when drowning overtook him, he said, "I believe..." (90)﴾ [Yunus]. Al-idrak (overtaking): the intention of the one who seeks to reach a thing. Drowning is a meaning, so how does the meaning turn into a thing that pursues Pharaoh?

Yes, it is as if drowning were one of the soldiers, possessing a mind that acts; it runs toward events: ﴿... until, when drowning overtook him, he said, "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am among the Muslims." (90)﴾ [Yunus]. Faith, when mentioned unqualified, is faith in the Supreme Power, as evidenced by the saying of the Truth, glory be to Him: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed, but say, 'We have submitted'..." (14)﴾ [al-Hujurat]. For faith requires the submission of the heart, while Islam requires adherence to the pillars of Islam. Faith, as the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Say, I believe in Allah, then be upright." (5) In this statement there is a specific mention that faith is directed only to Allah, the Most High.

But if you say, for example: "I believe that you are a good man," this is faith with an object. But when faith is mentioned without qualification, it refers to faith in Allah, the Most High. Therefore Allah, glory be to Him, said to the Bedouins: ﴿But say, "We have submitted..." (14)﴾ [al-Hujurat].

Here comes the statement on the tongue of Pharaoh: ﴿... "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am among the Muslims." (90)﴾ [Yunus].

The disagreement here was between Pharaoh as the side of disbelief, and Musa and Harun and their people as the side of faith. Pharaoh declared his faith and said also: ﴿... and I am among the Muslims (90)﴾ [Yunus], but Allah did not accept this from him, as evidenced by the saying of the Truth, glory be to Him: ﴿"Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters? (91)"﴾

1 Ittaba'ahum: followed their trail in order to overtake them. Musa and his people, the Children of Israel, in their departure were six hundred and twenty thousand, and Pharaoh followed them at sunrise with two million six hundred thousand. Baghyan wa 'adwan: that is, in a state of insolence, wrongdoing and aggression. The exegetes said: bagh'yan: seeking exaltation without right in speech, and 'adwan in action. Adrakahu al-gharaq: reached him and overtook him. Qala amantu: that is, I believed, or "I believe" – and faith is of no benefit at that time, while repentance is accepted before the sight of the punishment. [Mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (4/3304, 3305), with adaptation.]
2 Al-istitrad: several tubes of different sizes and shapes, connected to one another by a horizontal tube; when liquid is placed in one of these tubes, the surface of the liquid rises to one horizontal level in all the tubes. [al-Mu'jam al-Wasit, Arabic Language Academy.]
3 Al-Zuhri said: rahwan, calm, is a description of Musa; that is, "at your ease." He said: and better than this is to make rahwan a description of the sea, because he went and left it calm, its water still, and said to Musa: leave the sea standing, its water still, and cross the sea yourself. [Mentioned by Ibn Manzur in al-Lisan, root r-h-y.] So His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And leave the sea calm (rahwan)... (24)﴾ [al-Dukhan], that is, its waves still, so that they may be deceived and descend into it.
4 "And I am among the Muslims": that is, among the monotheists who submit in obedience and surrender. This is a very late statement, which came after the time had passed.
5 On the authority of Sufyan ibn Abdullah al-Thaqafi, who said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, tell me a saying about Islam about which I will not ask anyone after you." He said: "Say, I believe in Allah, then be upright." Recorded by Muslim in his Sahih (38), and Ahmad in his Musnad (4/385).
6 It is said: this is the words of Allah, the Exalted. It is said: it is the words of Jibril. It is said: Mika'il, or other angels, peace be upon them. It is said: it is the words of Pharaoh within himself; there was no statement by the tongue, but rather it occurred in his heart, and he said within himself what he said, when repentance no longer benefited him. Its parallel is: ﴿We feed you only for the sake of Allah... (9)﴾ [al-Insan], where the Lord, glory be to Him, praised them for what was in their inner selves, not because they uttered it with their tongues. The speech here is the speech of the heart. [Mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir, 4/3306, with adaptation.]

This means: "Do you now say that you have believed and that you are among the Muslims?" Your statement is rejected, because it came at a time other than its proper time. There is a difference between the faith of compulsion (iman al-ijbar) and the faith of choice (iman al-ikhtiyar). Do you say now, "I have believed," when you have disobeyed before and used to cause corruption on the earth?

It would have been possible for Allah, glorified is He, to accept his faith while he was in a high place far from the evil that encompassed him.

Al-Haqq, glorified is He, does not accept the faith of anyone whose soul has reached the throat (al-hulqum). That is faith of compulsion, not faith of choice.

And if what were required were the faith of compulsion, Allah, glorified is He, would have compelled all creation to believe, and no one would have been able to disbelieve in Allah, the Exalted. Before us, the whole universe is subject to the command of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and no one in it refuses Allah, the Exalted.

The absolute power of al-Haqq, Mighty and Majestic is He, is able to compel mankind to believe, but that establishes the absoluteness of His power, not the beloved-ness of the Worshipped to the worshipper.

This beloved-ness of the Worshipped is established only if you have a choice in whether you believe or do not believe. Allah, glorified is He, wants the faith of choice (iman al-ikhtiyar).[3]

So, what was rejected from Pharaoh was not the statement, but the time of the statement.

It is said that it was rejected and not accepted, despite his saying it three times, because the people of Musa at that time had entered the stage of anthropomorphizing the Essence of Allah, and they claimed, may Allah forbid, that Allah, exalted is He above what they say, sat on a rock and lowered His feet into a pool of water, and used to play with the fish... and so on, the fables that the Children of Israel invented.

When Pharaoh declared that he believed in the God in whom the Children of Israel believed, this means that he did not believe in the true God, glorified is He.

[1] al-Najwa: what is raised above the earth.
[2] Haaqa bihi al-shay' yahiqu haiqan: it befell him and encompassed him. It was said: al-hayq in the language is that the consequence of a harm one has done envelops a person. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿So Allah protected him from the evils of what they schemed, and there befell the people of Pharaoh an evil torment﴾ [Ghafir 45], and Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿...when they were denying the signs of Allah, and there befell them what they used to mock﴾ [al-Ahqaf 26]..
[3] Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them entirely. Then, would you compel the people until they become believers?﴾ [Yunus 99].

Thereafter the Truthful One (Allah, glorified is He) says:

﴿So today We shall save you in your body, that you may be a sign for those who come after you. Indeed, many of the people are heedless of Our signs.﴾ (10:92)

We know that the human being is composed of a body, which is the material frame formed in the shape we know, and within the body there is the soul (rūḥ), by which movement and life come about.

When we say "body" (badan), understand that it is stripped of the soul, just as we say "jasad" (corpse/physical form). And when the word "jasad" is used absolutely, its meaning is the material frame stripped of the soul.

The Truthful One says:

﴿And We did test Solomon and placed upon his throne a body (jasad)...﴾ (38:34)

Our master Solomon, peace be upon him, enjoyed what Allah had given him of dominion, the like of which is not fitting for anyone after him. Allah subjected to him the jinn and the winds and taught him all languages. He was the possessor of commands, prohibitions and authority. Then he found himself sitting on his throne without movement and without a soul, and any one of his subjects could approach him. Then Allah returned his soul to his body, and this is what the Truthful One refers to when He says:

﴿...then he turned back (anāba)﴾ (38:34). That is: he came to himself and knew that all he possessed was a bestowal poured upon him, not a matter springing from his own essence.

Now, in the noble verse we are presently concerned with, the Truthful One says:

﴿So today We shall save you in your body, that you may be a sign for those who come after you...﴾ (10:92)

By Allah, if the Truthful One had not commanded the sea to cast up the corpse of Pharaoh, would it not have been possible for them to say that he was a god and that he would return once more?

But the Truthful One willed that the sea should cast up his body as it casts up the carcass of any drowned animal, so that there would be no doubt that this Pharaoh had drowned, and so that those of his people who remained might look upon his reality and know that he was merely a human being, and he would become a lesson for all, after he had been a tyrant, a profligate despot who said to them:

﴿I know of no god for you other than myself...﴾ (28:38)

Some historians of ancient times say that the Pharaoh intended is Thutmose, and that they examined part of his body and found in it traces of salt water.

We say: Pharaoh is not the name of a person but a designation of an office. Perhaps the mummified bodies of the Pharaohs tell us that the reason for preserving the bodies is a lesson; let every person take heed and see how civilizations collapsed, and how those bodies remained a sign by which we take warning.

The Qur'an has addressed the matter of Pharaoh, and the Truthful One says:

﴿And Pharaoh of the stakes (dhī al-awtād)﴾ (89:10). And He says in the same surah concerning every oppressive corrupter:

﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful (la-bi'l-mirṣād)﴾ (89:14). We observe that the Truthful One's speech about Pharaoh in Surat al-Fajr was speech that joined to the civilization of the Pharaohs other ancient civilizations, such as the civilization of 'Ād and the civilization of Thamūd.

Likewise the Truthful One spoke of Pharaoh in the course of the scenes of the story of Moses, peace be upon him. But the account differs in the story of Joseph, peace be upon him: the office of Pharaoh does not appear there; rather the Truthful One speaks to us of other offices, namely the office of "the Governor of Egypt" (ʿazīz Miṣr), that is, its prime minister. And Allah speaks to us of the king of Egypt in His saying:

﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me..."﴾ (12:50). The difference between the office of "Pharaoh" and the office of "king" in Egyptian history was not discovered until the French expedition came to Egypt and Champollion deciphered the hieroglyphic script through the inscriptions of the Rosetta Stone. We learned that the rulers of ancient Egypt were called "Pharaohs" except in a period when Egypt was under the rule of the "Shepherd Kings" or the "Hyksos," who raided Egypt, ruled it as kings, and put an end to the rule of the Pharaohs; then the Pharaohs returned to rule Egypt after they had freed it from the domination of the Hyksos.

Thus we find that the Qur'an's reference in the story of Joseph, peace be upon him, was to the king, and it did not mention Pharaoh there. This is evidence that the Qur'an had, by its knowledge, preceded any discovery, and whenever a new discovery or genuine innovation comes, we find it confirming the Book of Allah.

The Truthful One concludes the verse about which our reflections are concerned with His saying:

﴿...And indeed many of the people are heedless of Our signs.﴾ (10:92)

This saying makes clear that there are those who are heedless of the signs and there are those who are not heedless of them; they look upon these signs, contemplate them and reflect on them, and inquire into the benefit of everything, and so they arrive at innovations and inventions from which mankind benefits; the birth of these is announced by searching for them, so that the greatness of Allah in His creation may become manifest.

When a person looks at those innovations, he will find them to be the offspring of ideas of those who looked carefully and possessed the capacity of deduction. Had people not been heedless of contemplating the signs of the universe, the heavens and the earth, the innovations and inventions would have increased. The Truthful One says:

﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth do they pass by, while they turn away from it?﴾ (12:105)

When we look at the discoverer of the law of gravity, Newton, who saw an apple fall from its tree, we find that tens of thousands or millions of human beings had witnessed before him the sight of a fruit falling from a tree, but Newton alone reflected and contemplated what was happening before him until he was guided to the discovery of the law of gravity.

After Newton came those who built spacecraft that benefit from this law and others.

Likewise we find those who designed submarines and gigantic ships resembling floating cities; these relied upon the one who discovered the law of "buoyancy" and the principle of "Archimedes," who observed that whenever something is immersed in water, the water rises by the same volume as the immersed object.

All of these discovered—they did not create—secrets that were present in the universe, and they were distinguished by their attentiveness to them.

Likewise the scientist who discovered "penicillin" observed that from a pot (aṣīṣ) of organic material drops of mouldy water were falling, and he saw that insects approaching this water died. He took a sample of this mould and began conducting some experiments on it in his laboratory until he discovered "penicillin."

The saying of the Truthful One: ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth do they pass by, while they turn away from it?﴾ (12:105). It is as though, had they not turned away, they would have deduced a great deal from the signs of the universe.

Likewise the stories that come in the Qur'an came only so that people might take heed and reflect. When Allah sends a messenger supported by a miracle from Him that human beings cannot match, then people should submit and say, "We believe," and not remain in a state of repeating earlier experiments; for the advancement of mankind in material matters has continued, because each generation of scientists takes the results of knowledge reached by those who preceded them. So why should this not happen in matters of belief?

Had people begun from where others ended, we would have found every believer in Allah, and every child would have taken up the matter from where his father ended, and the goodness of Adam would have reached everyone born thereafter. But the affliction of mankind is that a person wants to test things for himself.

We find this in harmful matters such as wine: we find it harmful to everyone who approaches it; yet when religion forbids it, we find someone asking, "Why is it forbidden?"

Likewise smoking: we find someone who tries it although the earlier experiments have proven its grave harms. Had every person taken the experiences of those before him, he would have added his life to the lives of others.

(1) anāba: returned to Allah in repentance. [Kalimāt al-Qur'ān, Shaykh Ḥasanayn Muḥammad Makhlūf]

(2) nunajjīka: We will bring you out of the sea. bi-badanika: with your body, which has no soul in it. li-takūna li-man khalfaka: after you. āyah: a lesson, so that they may know your servanthood and not undertake an act like yours. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that some of the Children of Israel doubted his death, so he was brought out for them so that they might see him. [Tafsir al-Jalalayn, p. 187]. Al-Yazīdī and Ibn al-Samīʿ read "nunaḥḥīka" with a ḥāʾ, meaning: you will be on a side of the sea so that they may see you.

(3) It was said regarding the meaning of dhū al-awtād: because Pharaoh used to torture people with four stakes [Mukhtaṣar Tafsir al-Ṭabarī, p. 513]. It is mentioned in Tafsir al-Jalalayn (p. 398) that Pharaoh would stake out, for everyone with whom he was angry, four stakes to which he would tie his hands and feet and torture him. In [Kalimāt al-Qur'ān, Shaykh Ḥasanayn Muḥammad Makhlūf]: the awtād are the armies or the strong structures.

(4) inna rabbaka la-bi'l-mirṣād: He watches their deeds and recompenses them for them. [Kalimāt al-Qur'ān].

(5) wa-inna kathīran min al-nās: i.e., the people of Makkah. ʿan āyātinā ghāfilūn: they do not take heed from them. [Tafsir al-Jalalayn p. 187].

(6) ka-ayyin min āyah: how many a sign—many signs. [Kalimāt al-Qur'ān].

(7) al-aṣṣ (with fatḥ, kasr, or ḍamm on the hamza): the base. al-aṣīṣ: the base of a jar (dann), i.e., its bottom; it is said: it is like a jar having two handles in which a pot is carried. In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: al-aṣīṣ is what has broken of vessels, and it is half a jar or a earthenware vessel in which fragrant plants are grown. [Lisān al-ʿArab, root ʼ-ṣ-ṣ]. This word is also applied to earthenware vessels made specially for growing flowers and plants.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 10, verse 93:

The Truthful Lord then says:

﴿And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good settlement, and We provided for them of the good things. And they did not differ until knowledge had come to them. Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ.﴾ (93)

The word "tabawwa'" means to establish a mubaa'a, that is, the houses in which one has a private dwelling. When the word "mubaw'a" is used without qualification, it means a region or a homeland.

The homeland is where you move about, and so does everyone else; the house, however, belongs to the person and his family as a private dwelling.

As for the wealthy man, he may have a private wing in the house. He may set aside in his home one wing for himself, another for his son, and a third for his daughter.

As for the majority of people, each family lives in an "apartment" that may consist of one, two or three rooms, according to the family's means.

Thus there is a difference between settling in houses (tabawwu' al-buyut) and settling in lands (tabawwu' al-mawatin). The settling of a homeland is the homeland itself.

The Truthful Lord had already said to Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them: ﴿That you two settle your people in Egypt in houses..﴾ (87) [Yunus]. This was the private settling. As for the general settling, it requires the power of the Exalted Lord, and He says here: ﴿And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good settlement..﴾ (93) [Yunus].

The Truthful Lord granted them this in the time of Moses, peace be upon him, and granted them residence in Egypt and al-Sham. He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed..﴾ (1) [al-Isra'] Since the Truthful Lord has blessed its surroundings, there must be much good in it, and the land around it must be a good settlement.

The word "al-sidq" (truthfulness) means the sum of goodness and righteousness. For this reason we find that when the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, was asked: "Can a believer be a coward?" he said: "Yes." When he was asked: "Can a believer be stingy?" he said: "Yes." When he was asked: "Can a believer be a liar?" he said: "No" (3).

Therefore in Islam there is a punishment for fornication and a punishment imposed on the thief (4), whereas lying is a trait the Muslim does not approach, because he must be truthful. All the qualities of goodness are a good settlement.

For this reason we find the saying of the Truthful Lord: ﴿And say: "My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and cause me to exit a sound exit" (5)..﴾ (80) [al-Isra'].

And the saying of the Truthful Lord: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe that they will have a sure precedence with their Lord (6)..﴾ (2) [Yunus].

And the saying of the Truthful Lord: ﴿And grant me a tongue of truth among the later generations (7)﴾ (84) [al-Shu'ara']. That is: grant me a good remembrance, so that it is not said that so-and-so was a liar. As for "qadam sidq" (a sure precedence), it refers to the precedences of goodness that one strives to attain. Therefore the reward for truthfulness is what the Truthful Lord describes: ﴿In an assembly of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, Omnipotent (8)﴾ (55) [al-Qamar]. It is an assembly in the presence of a King who is not stingy, and no one sits in His courts except one whom He loves, and He does not withhold His goodness from those who are in His courts.

The seat of truth is the reward for one whose Lord has responded to him, so He caused him to enter a sound entrance, caused him to exit a sound exit, granted him a tongue of truth, and a sure precedence.

After the Truthful Lord settled the Children of Israel in a good settlement, in Egypt and al-Sham, and after He had said to them: ﴿Go down to a city, for indeed you will have what you ask (9)..﴾ (61) [al-Baqara], that is: the Truthful Lord fulfilled His saying: ﴿And provided for them of the good things..﴾ (93) [Yunus], and rescued them from Pharaoh, and it was to be expected that their affairs would be set right.

The Lord says: ﴿And they did not differ until knowledge had come to them..﴾ (93) [Yunus]. What is meant by this is their recognition of the signs of the final Messenger, Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace. Some of them awaited the coming of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, in order to believe in him, and some of them persisted in rebellion. Therefore God, glorified is He, cut them into groups among the nations.

When we look at the precision of the Qur'anic expression, we find that it specifies this matter of fragmentation: they represent a piece in every nation. That is, He, glorified is He, did not dissolve them among the peoples; rather, in every land they went to they have a place of their own, and they do not melt into others.

The Truthful Lord says: ﴿And We said after him (10) to the Children of Israel: "Dwell in the land..﴾ (104) [al-Isra']. Some superficial person may say: Is there any dwelling other than on the earth?

We say: We may note that the Truthful Lord did not specify in any verse the particular spot of earth where they would dwell. It is as if the Truthful Lord has explained the judgment He issued against them, that they would be scattered in the earth as nations. He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And We divided them in the earth into nations (11)..﴾ (168) [al-A'raf].

If we see them in our present days, and they have now a homeland, know that the Truthful Lord is the one who said: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture: "You will surely cause corruption in the earth twice, and you will surely reach great haughtiness."﴾ (4) [al-Isra'].

He also said at the end of Surat al-Isra': ﴿And We said after him to the Children of Israel: "Dwell in the land, and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you as a mixed multitude (12)"﴾ (104) [al-Isra']. Bringing them as a mixed multitude means gathering them into a national homeland, so that the crushing blow which the Truthful Lord mentioned in His saying may come upon them: ﴿..So when the promise of the Hereafter came, to sadden your faces and to enter the Mosque as they entered it the first time, and to destroy what they had conquered with complete destruction (13)﴾ (7) [al-Isra']. For we will not be able to fight them in every country where God has scattered them, but when they gather in one place, it becomes easy for God's decree to descend upon them.

When we look at their journey, we find that Yathrib was the place that opened up to them after the persecutions of the societies they had entered. When they gathered in Yathrib, they gained prestige, because they were people of knowledge, people of economics, and people of war.

They gathered in Medina because the sincere People of the Book informed them that this city was the place of emigration of a prophet and messenger who would come from the Arabs at the end of time. So they remained there, awaiting him, and they used to say to the disbelievers of Quraysh: "A time has drawn near in which a prophet will come whom we will follow, and we will kill you with him, killing as the 'Ad and Iram were killed" (14).

It was expected that they would believe in his message, may God bless him and grant him peace, but as soon as the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, appeared with the light of his message, they denied him out of fear for their temporal authority.

This is what the noble verse that is the subject of our reflections speaks of: ﴿And they did not differ until knowledge had come to them..﴾ (93) [Yunus]. That is: their knowledge of the coming of the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, was the source of their difference. Some of them heard hints about him, may God bless him and grant him peace, and recognized his signs, and so they believed in him; and some of them did not believe in him.

Previously they had not differed and were united, and they threatened the polytheists of Quraysh. When the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, appeared and al-Aws and al-Khazraj learned of him, that he was a messenger of God, Exalted, who had appeared in Mecca, al-Aws and al-Khazraj said: "This is the prophet with whom the Jews threatened us. Come, let us go and get ahead of them to him before they get ahead of us and kill us with him."

Thus it was the Jews who were the cause of the Prophet's emigration, may God bless him and grant him peace, to Medina, because al-Aws and al-Khazraj got ahead of them to him. This is so that we may know how God, Exalted, supports His religion through its enemies.

For this reason we find that in their disagreement, Abdullah ibn Salam (15) came to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and said: "The Jews are a people of slander, and if I believe in you, O Messenger of God, they will say about me what will harm me; so before I announce my Islam, ask them about me."

Ibn Salam, in this, was following a course consistent with his being a Jew. When the company of Jews gathered, the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, asked them and said: "What do you say about Ibn Salam?"

They said: "He is our rabbi and our elder, and the most scrupulous among us." After they praised him greatly, Ibn Salam said: "O Messenger of God, I bear witness that there is no god but God and that you are the Messenger of God."

At this the Jews began to heap abuse upon him, and Ibn Salam said: "Did I not tell you, O Messenger of God, that they are a people of slander?" (16)

So the meaning of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And they did not differ until knowledge had come to them..﴾ (93) [Yunus], is that some people among them remained upon falsehood, and some of them believed in the true Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace.

The Truthful Lord concludes the noble verse with His saying: ﴿..Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ (93)﴾ [Yunus]. That is: God, glorified and exalted, will judge between those who came into the ranks of faith and those who remained in a zealous Judaism opposed to faith.

We note that the word "baynahum" (between them) shows that the pronoun is general, referring to these and to those.

We say: God, glorified and exalted, judges on the Day of Resurrection between believers and disbelievers, and He also judges between disbelievers. Among them were those who wronged other disbelievers, and among them were embezzlers and bribe-takers, and among them were those who acted contrary to the requirements of their religion; therefore God, glorified is He, judges between them.

The verse indicates generality in judgment, past, present and future, between every believer and disbeliever, and between every penitent and sinner.

1 Abuwa-na: We caused to descend. Mubaw'a sidq: an abode of honour, namely Egypt and al-Sham. Fa-ma ikhtalafu: in that some of them believed and some of them disbelieved. [Tafsir al-Jalalayn: p. 187, adapted].
.
2 Subhana alladhi asra bi-'abdihi: exalting and declaring God free, glorified is He, from what the polytheists say about Him. Al-isra' and al-sura: travelling by night. Al-Masjid al-Aqsa: Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Alladhi barakna hawlahu: for its inhabitants in their livelihoods and sustenance. [Mukhtasar Tafsir al-Tabari: p. 313].
3 Related by Imam Malik in his Muwatta' (p. 990) from the hadith of Safwan ibn Sulaym, as a mursal report.
4 The Book and the Sunnah have established specific punishments for specific crimes, namely the crimes of the hadd (fixed penalties): fornication, slander, theft, drunkenness, waging war, apostasy, and rebellion; this is to safeguard society in respect of: religion, reason, property, honour, and life. Each of these crimes has conditions that must be fulfilled for its specific punishment to be carried out. For the details of this, consult the books of jurisprudence (chapters on hudud).
5 "And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance": that is, cause me to enter Medina with an entry that is pleasing, in which I see nothing I dislike. "And cause me to exit": from Mecca, an exit by which I do not turn my heart back toward it. [Tafsir al-Jalalayn: p. 251].
6 Qadam sidq: a precedence of virtue and an exalted rank. [Kalimat al-Qur'an, by Shaykh Husayn Muhammad Makhluf].
7 Lisan sidq: good praise and a beautiful remembrance. [Kalimat al-Qur'an].
8 Maq'ad sidq: a pleasing place. [Kalimat al-Qur'an]. "Inda malik": with a possessor of dominion. Muqtadir: over all that He wills, there is no god but Him. [Mukhtasar Tafsir al-Tabari: p. 607].
9 Ihbitu: descend. Misran: one of the cities, that is, a town among the towns.
10 Min ba'dihi: that is, after the drowning of Pharaoh.
11 That is: We divided them in the earth into divisions. [Tafsir al-Jalalayn: p. 146].
12 Lafifan: all together.
13 That is: if you corrupt the second time, and your enemies come to sadden your faces, that is, to humiliate and subdue you, "and to enter the Mosque" (7), that is, Bayt al-Maqdis, "as they entered it the first time" (7), that is, in which they roamed through the homes, "and to destroy what they had conquered with complete destruction" (7), that is, to ruin and devastate what they had gained power over. Adapted from Tafsir Ibn Kathir (3/26), in which Ibn Kathir cites Qatadah's saying: The Children of Israel have returned, so God has empowered over them this group, Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, and his companions, who take the jizya from them by hand while they are humbled. This does not preclude that it happens several times; for this reason the Lord of Glory said: ﴿And if you return, We will return (8)﴾ [al-Isra'].
14 The Truthful Lord says: ﴿And when there came to them a Book from God confirming what was with them, and before that they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved, but when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it. So the curse of God is upon the disbelievers (89)﴾ [al-Baqara]. And from elders of the Ansar who said: We had overpowered them by force for ages in the Jahiliyyah, and we were people of polytheism while they were people of the Book, and they used to say: A prophet is about to be sent now, we will follow him; his time has drawn near, and we will kill you with him as 'Ad and Iram were killed. Then when God sent His Messenger from Quraysh and we followed him, they disbelieved in him. Related by Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir (1/124), citing Ibn Ishaq.
15 He is Abdullah ibn Salam ibn al-Harith al-Isra'ili, Abu Yusuf. He embraced Islam when the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, arrived in Medina. His name had been al-Husayn, and the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, named him Abdullah. He witnessed with Umar the conquest of Bayt al-Maqdis and al-Jabiyah. When the strife between Ali and Mu'awiyah occurred, he took a wooden sword, withdrew from it, and remained in Medina until he died in the year 43 AH. (al-A'lam, by al-Zirikli, 4/90).
16 From Anas ibn Malik: that Abdullah ibn Salam heard of the Prophet's arrival in Medina, so he came to him asking about certain things. He said: "I will ask you about three things that none but a prophet knows: What is the first sign of the Hour? What is the first food the people of Paradise eat? And why does the child resemble its father or its mother?" He said: "Jibril informed me of it just now." Ibn Salam said: "That is the enemy of the Jews among the angels." He said: "As for the first sign of the Hour, it is a fire that will gather them from the east to the west. As for the first food the people of Paradise eat, it is the caudate lobe of the fish's liver. As for the child, if the man's fluid precedes the woman's, the child resembles the man, and if the woman's fluid precedes the man's, the child resembles the woman." He said: "I bear witness that there is no god but God, and that you are the Messenger of God." He said: "O Messenger of God, the Jews are a people of slander, so ask them about me before they learn of my Islam." The Jews came, and the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "What kind of man is Abdullah ibn Salam among you?" They said: "The best of us and the son of the best of us, and the most excellent of us and the son of the most excellent of us." The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "What do you think if Abdullah ibn Salam embraces Islam?" They said: "May God protect him from that." He repeated it to them, and they gave the same answer. Then Abdullah came out to them and said: "I bear witness that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God." They said: "He is the worst of us and the son of the worst of us," and they disparaged him. He said: "This is what I was afraid of, O Messenger of God." Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (3938) and Ahmad in his Musnad (3/272, 271, 108).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 10, verse 94:

Then the Truthful One (al-Haqq, subhanahu) says:

﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who recite the Book before you. The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾ (94):

The address here is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the meaning is other than him. We know that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said from the beginning that he had no doubt about his message, and when his people offered him sovereignty he said: "By Allah, if they placed the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left on condition that I abandon this matter, until Allah makes it prevail or I perish in it, I would not abandon it."

We say: Almighty Allah includes the address to the community (ummah) within the address to His Messenger (ﷺ), because when the followers read and hear the address, and it is directed in this manner to the Messenger (ﷺ), they will not disdain (istinkaf) any command that is issued to them.

An example of this: if a commander issues an order to two of his assistants who lead two groups of fighters, and the supreme commander says to each of them: "Beware of doing such and such, or making such and such." The supreme commander, by his instructions, does not intend his assistants, but intends all of their subordinate soldiers.

The command here came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) so that his community would understand that the Messenger (ﷺ) would never refuse any of Allah's commands, rather he (ﷺ) executes precisely everything he is commanded; this is by way of addressing the community through the person of its Messenger (ﷺ).

As for the saying of the Truthful One: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who recite the Book before you...﴾ (94): this statement is evidence that those who had knowledge of the Book from the earlier (peoples) before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) know the clear realities about his message (ﷺ).

Those who are arrogant and disbelieve in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his message know him only as they know their own sons. 'Abdullah ibn Salam said: "I recognized Muhammad when I saw him as I recognize my son, and my recognition of Muhammad is even stronger."

So the truth is clear to them, written in the Torah as glad tidings of him (ﷺ), and this proves that you, O Muhammad, are truthful in your call, by the testimony of these people.

The Truthful One concludes the verse with His saying: ﴿...The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾ (94): The truth coming from Almighty Allah is established and does not change, because it is a fact, and a fact does not multiply, but comes in one form.

As for falsehood, it comes in multiple forms.

Therefore the duty of the careful investigator is to turn over the aspects of the testimonies given before him in the prosecution or the court, so that his judgment comes out correct, with no room for contradiction, and without relying on imagination or lies.

The saying of the Truthful One: ﴿The truth has certainly come to you...﴾ (94) indicates only that those who read the Book have known that you are truly the Messenger of Allah, and some of them left the camp of Judaism and came to the camp of faith in you, because the truth that has come has no human input in it, but has come from your Lord:

﴿...so do not be among the doubters.﴾ (94): The arrival of the address in this form is, as I have said, directed to the believing community in the person of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

And the Truthful One says: ﴿If you associate (others with Allah), your deeds will surely be nullified...﴾ (65) [az-Zumar]: This statement was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is not reasonable that the Prophet (ﷺ) would associate partners with Allah; every verse bearing the meaning of guidance in matters from which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is free is specifically for his community.

Also the Truthful One says: ﴿And do not be among those who denied the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.﴾ (95) [Yunus]: A wise statement, when directed toward good, may come with its opposite of evil, so that things become clear by comparison.

In our daily lives we find a father saying to his son: "Work hard at your lessons, and listen well to your teachers so that you succeed, and do not be like so-and-so who failed." The father in this case brings the good encouragement and accompanies it with its opposite, which is the warning against evil.

And a poet said:
The face is like white dawn, and the hair is like black night.
Two opposites, when brought together in beauty, the opposite makes the beauty of the other appear.

1 The one addressed in this verse is Muhammad (ﷺ), and what is meant is other than him; likewise the verse after it: ﴿And do not be among those who denied the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.﴾ (95). Some scholars have interpreted "doubt" here as constriction of the chest, i.e., if your chest is constricted by the disbelief of these people, then be patient, and ask those who recite the Book before you; they will inform you of the patience of the prophets before you under the harm of their peoples and how their final outcome was. [Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/3310]..
2 "So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who recite the Book before you": from the people of the Torah and the Gospel, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam. It is said that when this verse was revealed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I do not doubt, nor do I ask." Allah knew this about him. The manner of this statement is like a man's saying to his son: "If you are my son, then be dutiful to me" (from al-barr), meaning: be dutiful to me. He does not doubt that he is his son. "Among the doubters": the skeptics. [Mukhtasar Tafsir al-Tabari: p. 241]..
3 "Imtara fi al-shay'": he doubted the thing and did not become certain of it. "Tamara al-qawm bihi": they disputed it. "Tamara fi al-shay'": he was skeptical about it. The Most High says: ﴿Then which of the favors of your Lord would you dispute?﴾ (55) [an-Najm], meaning: doubt, and it includes the meaning of denial. [al-Qamus al-Qawim]; see Lisan al-Arab, root m-r-y.
4 Ibn Hisham cited it in al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (1/266) attributed to Ibn Ishaq: the Quraysh said to Abu Talib: "O Abu Talib, you have age, nobility and standing among us, and we have asked you to restrain your nephew from us, but you have not restrained him; so either we will confront him and you over this until one of the two groups perishes." Abu Talib sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said to him: "O nephew, your people have come to me and said such and such; spare me and yourself, and do not burden me with what I cannot bear." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him this statement..
5 Istinkaf: refraining out of arrogance and pride. From it the saying of the Most High: ﴿The Messiah will never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor will the angels brought near. And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant - He will gather them to Himself all together.﴾ (172) [an-Nisa'].
6 Its confirmation is the saying of the Most High: ﴿So for that, invite, and remain steadfast as you were commanded, and do not follow their desires, and say: I believe in what Allah has sent down of Book, and I have been commanded to act justly between you...﴾ (15) [ash-Shura].
7 Ibn Kathir mentioned in his tafsir (2/194) that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab asked 'Abdullah ibn Salam: "Do you know Muhammad as you know your son?" He said: "Yes, and more. The trustworthy one (al-Amin) descended from heaven upon the trustworthy one on earth with his description, so I recognized him; and as for his mother, I do not know what she did."..
8 The Most High says: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written in what they have of the Torah and the Gospel, who enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong and makes lawful for them the good things and prohibits for them the evil and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them. So those who believed in him, honored him, supported him, and followed the light which was sent down with him - it is those who will be the successful.﴾ (157) [al-A'raf].
And on the authority of 'Ata' ibn Yasar, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, who used to say: This verse in the Qur'an: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness and a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ (45) [al-Ahzab] is in the Torah: "O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings, a warner, and a guardian for the unlettered. You are My servant and My messenger; I have named you al-Mutawakkil. You are not harsh, nor coarse, nor shouting in the markets, and you do not repel evil with evil, but you pardon and forgive. We will not take him until We have set straight through him the crooked community, until they say: There is no god but Allah, and by it they open blind eyes, deaf ears, and veiled hearts." Narrated by al-Bukhari in the Book of Tafsir (8/585 Fath) and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il (1/375)..
9 I.e., if you associate anyone with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified. [Mukhtasar Tafsir al-Tabari: p. 527], adapted. The nullification of deeds (hubut) is their invalidation and corruption despite their having been done; its root is when livestock "habitat" (ḥabiṭat al-māshiyah), i.e., they eat so much that their bellies swell and what is in them does not come out. [See Lisan al-Arab, root h-b-t]..
10 Opposites: in their appearance the features within them appear; we do not know the value of truth except when we have tasted the bitterness of falsehood, and we do not know the value of day except when night has covered us in its darkness, and we do not know the beauty of justice except when we have been burned by the fire of injustices..

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 10, verse 95:

The Truthful (Allah) then says:

﴿So do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.﴾ (95)

The signs of Allah (ayat Allah), as we know, are of several kinds. There are cosmic signs (ayat kawniyyah), which are the foundation of the first belief that their Creator is the Most High Creator, and these signs draw attention to the wondrous craftsmanship of Allah, the precision of His creation, and the all-encompassing scope of His power.

Likewise, the signs are intended as the miracles sent down upon the Messengers, peace be upon them, to show the truthfulness of each Messenger in conveying from Allah, the Exalted.

And the signs of the Noble Qur'an, which carry the method (manhaj) of Allah.

And they used to deny all of the signs.

The address in this verse is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it comes as a conjunction with what is in the preceding verse, where the Truthful says: ﴿If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you... (94)﴾ [Yunus]. Whatever comes of such a statement, we must not understand from it that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) could possibly doubt, or that it is probable that he would be among those who denied the signs of Allah, the Exalted. Rather, the mention of such a matter is intended to remove the misgivings of humanity, whatever those misgivings may be. So when we find an address in the revelation whose intended target is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the ultimate purpose is to balance the measures of understanding in his community, through teaching and guidance, because the method was sent down to him to convey to his community, so he is a witness over the nations (1).

And since the preceding verse clarifies: "If you are in doubt, ask," He, the Exalted, gives him the question so that he may hear the answer from Him, and so that He may make it heard by the whole community: the answer that says, "I do not doubt and I do not ask, and what Allah the Exalted has sent down to me is sufficient for me."

Is it not mentioned in the Noble Qur'an that the Truthful, the Exalted, says to the angels on the Day of Resurrection, in the presence of those who worshipped the angels, addressing His angels and pointing to those who worshipped the angels: ﴿...Did these people use to worship you?﴾ (40) [Saba'], while we know that the angels: ﴿...do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and do what they are commanded﴾ (6) [al-Tahrim].

The Truthful knows in advance the answer of the angels, who say: ﴿Glory be to You; You are our Protector, not them...﴾ (41) [Saba']. But He, the Exalted, wished to let all in the gathering hear the answer of the angels as they deny that anyone among the creation should worship them; these people only worshipped the jinn.

So the question came in order to show the response to it, just as Jesus, peace be upon him, responds when he is worshipped by some of his people, and Allah asks him about that: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah...?"﴾ (116) [al-Ma'idah], and the answer comes: ﴿Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say...﴾ (116) [al-Ma'idah]. Thus the intended meaning is that the Messenger (ﷺ) should say: "I do not doubt and I do not ask."

Doubt (shakk) (2), as we know, means: the equal balance of the side of negation and the side of affirmation. If one of them outweighs the other, this is opinion (zann), and the outweighed one is delusion, fabrication and falsehood.

The word "shakk" is derived from a concrete matter. We see fishermen threading every fish after catching it onto a cord called "al-mushakkak."

Likewise we see someone who "joins" necklaces (al-'uqud) and he threads the bead onto the cord (3). From this we derive that doubt (shakk) means: joining one thing to another. From it come al-shakaik (4), which are houses arranged alongside one another.

And from it comes "shaak al-silah (5)," meaning one who joined himself to his armour.

So doubt is joining one thing to another, and in terms of lineage, it joins negation and affirmation together, because you are unable to prefer one of them.

Every address concerning doubt comes in this manner. The verse we are concerned with says: ﴿So do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.﴾ (95) [Yunus].

We know that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is himself one of the signs, and thus we see that the address is directed to his community. It is impossible that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would be among those who deny the signs of Allah, the Exalted, because denying the signs of Allah means turning truth into falsehood and turning reality into what is not reality.

Those who deny the signs are either those who do not believe in a God, or those who believe in God but do not believe in a Messenger, or those who believe in God and believe in a Messenger but do not believe in what was sent down to the Messenger (ﷺ).

What confirms this is a verse at the end of the surah in which the Truthful says: ﴿Say, "O people, if you are in doubt about my religion, then I do not worship those you worship besides (6) Allah...﴾ (104) [Yunus]. So it is as if the address intended is to the community.

(1) In confirmation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We have made you a median community, that you may be witnesses over the people and the Messenger may be a witness over you...﴾ (143) [al-Baqarah].

(2) Shakk: a psychological state in which the mind wavers between affirmation and negation, and stops short of judgment. [al-Mu'jam al-Wasit]

(3) Shakka al-shay' and ashtakkahu: he joined its parts. [al-Mu'jam al-Wasit: root sh-k-k]

(4) Al-shakak: the plural of shakika, a collection of things joined (shakka, i.e. joined) to one another. [al-Mu'jam al-Wasit: root sh-k-k]

(5) Al-shakk: what is worn or put on of weapons. [al-Mu'jam al-Wasit: root sh-k-k]

(6) Dun: the opposite of fawq (above). It may be used as an adverb, and it comes with the meaning of "in front of," "behind," "other than," "near or direction," "before," and "less." Distinguishing among these meanings is done by context. In the verse ﴿Say, "O people, if you are in doubt about my religion, then I do not worship those you worship besides Allah, but I worship Allah who takes your souls, and I have been commanded to be among the believers.﴾ (104) [Yunus], it means "other than." [al-Qamus al-Qawim], adapted.

And the saying of the Truthful, glorified is He, after that:

﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified (1) will not believe (96)﴾:

This statement makes clear to us that the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, has known with eternal knowledge that they will not direct their choice toward faith.

His judgment here does not negate from them the responsibility of choice; rather it is God's eternal knowledge of what they will do, and then they came upon choice, so God's knowledge of them was realized through their conduct.

His judgment, glorified is He, is based on choice, and it is an estimating judgment (ḥukm taqdīrī).

An example of this – and to God belongs the highest likeness – is when the Minister of Agriculture comes and announces that we have estimated the cotton crop this year, by calculating the area of land planted with cotton and the expected average per feddan. He may hit the target, and he may miss it as a result of the worlds and other circumstances surrounding cotton cultivation; the cotton may well be struck by one of the pests, such as the bollworm or the leaf worm.

So, in the human domain, an estimate may hit and may err, because man estimates without absolute knowledge, but with relative knowledge.

As for the estimation of the Truth, glorified is He, it is an eternal estimation, and when the Truth, glorified is He, estimates, what He has estimated must necessarily occur.

Therefore we must distinguish between a judgment of compelling necessity, over which man has no disposal, and a measure that God has decreed that man would do by his own choice; and this is the greatness of the knowledge of the Unseen.

An example of this is the conduct of Abu Lahab (2). A Qur'an was revealed concerning him that is recited: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he. His wealth will not avail him, nor what he gained﴾ [al-Masad]. The surah was revealed while Abu Lahab was still alive, because the Truth, glorified is He, had known from eternity that Abu Lahab's inclinations would not drive him to faith. Had Abu Lahab possessed a grain of intelligence, he would have come to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "You said about me that I would burn in the Fire, but here I am declaring that I bear witness that there is no god but God and I bear witness that you are the Messenger of God."

But Abu Lahab did not possess that intelligence; God had known from eternity that his inclinations would not drive him to Islam, just as they drove Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, the uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ), and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Khalid ibn al-Walid, and 'Amr ibn al-'As. The Islam of these, despite their standing against the Prophet (ﷺ), was a possibility.

People may make estimates, but such an estimate is only made according to the information available to them, and no person possesses cosmic eternal knowledge of his estimations; his knowledge is limited, and the matter may come out other than what he estimated, because man does not possess what he estimates.

Let no one say that God punishes after having decreed in advance; for the estimation of the Truth, glorified is He, springs from His eternal knowledge, and they were enjoyed the right of choice. God, glorified is He, is the One who says: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, among them are those who say, "Which of you has this increased in faith?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice. But as for those in whose hearts is disease, it adds defilement to their defilement and they die while they are disbelievers (125)﴾ [at-Tawbah].

1 Ḥuqqat: "the word of your Lord, the punishment, was made obligatory upon them" [Tafsir al-Jalalayn: p. 187].
2 Abu Lahab is one of the paternal uncles of the Messenger of God (ﷺ); his name was ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and his kunya was Abu ʿUtba. He was called Abu Lahab (Father of the Flame) because of the redness and brightness of his face, as though it were a flame.
The occasion of revelation of the surah in which he is mentioned: the Prophet (ﷺ) went out to al-Baṭḥā, climbed the mountain and called out: "Yā ṣabāḥāh!" Quraysh gathered to him, and he said: "Tell me, if I told you that the enemy would attack you at dawn or at dusk, would you believe me?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment." Abu Lahab said: "Ruin to you! Did you gather us for this?" Then God revealed: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab (1)﴾ to its end. Related by Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ (208) from Ibn ʿAbbās.
3 Tabbat: perished, or lost, or failed. [Kalimat al-Qur'an, Shaykh Ḥasanayn Muḥammad Makhlūf].
4 This is His saying: ﴿He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame (3)﴾ [al-Masad], i.e., he will be roasted in the fire of Hell.
5 Rijs: filth and stench, sensory and moral, and it is applied to what is considered abhorrent in the Sharia. Rijs and rijz have the same meaning, and rijs is applied to punishment because it is its cause. God says: ﴿He said, "There has certainly fallen upon you from your Lord rijs and wrath..." (71)﴾ [al-A'raf], i.e., punishment because of the rijs they had committed. [al-Qamus al-Qawim], adapted.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 10, verse 97:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And even if every sign came to them, until they see the painful punishment (97)﴾:

So, the coming of signs and their repetition will not benefit them in turning towards faith, because the Truth, glory be to Him, knows that they will turn, by their own choice, to disbelief. They had said, before this, what the Truth, glory be to Him, related in His Mighty Book: ﴿And they say, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth (90), or you have a garden of palm trees and grapevines and cause rivers to gush forth within them abundantly (91), or you cause the sky to fall upon us in fragments as you have claimed, or you bring Allah and the angels before us (92), or you have a house of gold, or you ascend into the sky. And we will not believe in your ascension until you bring down to us a book we can read." Say, "Exalted is my Lord! Am I but a human messenger?" (93)﴾ [al-Isra'].

It is as if the Truth, glory be to Him, commands His Messenger to say, clarifying: "I am not the one who sends down the signs; rather, the signs are from Allah, the Exalted." Then the Qur'an gives the reason why those signs that they requested were not sent down, so He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And We did not refrain from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them...﴾ (59) [al-Isra']. So many signs were sent down to those who preceded in obstinacy and opposition, and the offer of faith to him is met with a disbelief that fills his heart.

So if there is someone who seeks faith, let him approach the inquiry into faith without a prior belief, let him look at the matter, and let him enter into whatever his heart allows; and this free choice of the heart, not conditioned by a prior belief, is the summit of acceptance.

The Truth, glory be to Him, has spoken in the previous verses about Divine Oneness, about the miraculous signs, about the truthfulness of prophethood, and about the Resurrection. He has also related to us some of the stories of the procession of messengers: from Noah, peace be upon him, then He elaborated a little on the story of Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both, and then He will come after that with the story of Jonah, peace be upon him.

We observe that the Truth, glory be to Him, gave the story of Noah, peace be upon him, at length (7), then gave news of messengers about whom He told us nothing, then gave the story of Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both, and then He will come after that with the story of Jonah, peace be upon him. So the surah includes three messages: the message of Noah, the message of Moses and Aaron, and the message of Jonah, who is the messenger after whom the surah was named.

One may ask: Why did He mention these three in this surah?

I say: We have labored much, and with us many exegetes, to grasp the wisdom in that, and why the stories of Hud, Thamud and Shu'ayb did not come in this surah; there must have been a wisdom in that.

The wisdom that has become clear to us is that the Truth, glory be to Him, exalted, presents the procession of the message and the procession of the opponents of every messenger, and the outcome to which the enemies' affair came, and likewise the outcome to which the affair of the Messenger and of those who believed in him came.

We find that those whom Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned here were destroyed by a uniform kind of destruction: the destruction of the people of Noah was by drowning, and likewise the destruction of the people of Pharaoh was by drowning, and likewise the story of our master Jonah was connected with the sea, for the whale swallowed him and went along in the sea.

So, those messengers mentioned here were connected with water, whereas the rest of the messenger procession had no connection with water.

We know that water holds life and holds destruction, because the Giver of life gives life through a thing, and destroys by that very thing. It is as if the Truth, glory be to Him, shows us the wisdom: "I destroyed by drowning there, and I saved from drowning here."

So, the all-encompassing power of Divine capability is what prevails over this surah, just as the all-encompassing power appears in other domains and in other forms (8).

This surah was named after Jonah because the Truth, glory be to Him, sent him to more than a hundred thousand (9), and they are the only people in this context whom the Truth, glory be to Him, excepted from destruction. The people of Noah were drowned, and the people of Pharaoh were drowned; both denied the messengers, but the people of Jonah, as soon as they saw the force of punishment (10), believed, and Allah, glory be to Him, saved them.

The surah was named after the one who was saved, because he returned to the Truth, glory be to Him, before witnessing the punishment, whereas they only saw the harbingers of the punishment, so they saved themselves by faith.

Here the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Why was there not a city that believed so that its faith would benefit it, except the people of Jonah? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and gave them enjoyment for a time (98)﴾ (11) (12):

1 "And even if every sign came to them": then it would not benefit them at that time. [Tafsir al-Jalalayn: p. 187]..
2 Yanbu': the spring whose water does not run dry..
3 Kisafan: pieces. Kisf: a cloud broken into pieces, and from it the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And He makes it into fragments, and you see the rain coming out from within it..(48)﴾ [al-Rum]..
4 Qabilan: facing one another. The meaning is seeing them directly..
5 Zukhruf here means gold. Zukhruf also means adornment, and it may be intended as deception, forgery, and the embellishment of falsehood, from the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy: devils of mankind and jinn, inspiring to one another decorative speech as delusion..(112)﴾ [al-An'am]..
6 Yanbu'an: a spring gushing for us with water in this our land. Jannah: a garden. Fa-tafajjar al-anhar: in our land where we are. Khilaluha: meaning, among the palm trees and vines. Khilaluha: between them at their roots. Tafjiran: a torrent flowing between them. Kisafan: pieces. Qabilan: facing, or all together, so that we see them face to face. Zukhruf: gold. Tarqa: you ascend by a stairway into the sky. [Abridged Tafsir al-Tabari: pp. 324-325], adapted..
7 Ithnab (elaboration), musawah (equality) and ijaz (brevity) are among the arts of eloquence. Ithnab: explanation with abundance. Musawah: the wording equal to the meaning. Ijaz: few words for a great meaning; and every situation has its own speech. [Sharh Dala'il al-I'jaz], adapted..
8 Among the all-encompassing power is the employment of a thing in its opposite, like fire, whose function is burning, yet it was "coolness and safety" for our master Abraham. Water holds life and contains drowning, and salvation through it: Allah, glory be to Him, saved Moses, peace be upon him, and drowned Pharaoh by it..
9 He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more (147)﴾ [al-Saffat]. They were from the city of "Nineveh" opposite Mosul in present-day Iraq..
10 Ba's: punishment. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Thus did those before them deny, until they tasted Our might..(148)﴾ [al-An'am]. And He says: ﴿How many a city We destroyed, and Our might came upon it by night or while they were resting at midday (4)﴾ [al-A'raf]. Ba's also means the severity of war, as He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And the patient in adversity and hardship and at the time of battle..(177)﴾ [al-Baqarah]. Ba's also means strength. He, the Exalted, says of the people of Bilqis, queen of Sheba, when she consulted them about the matter of Solomon: ﴿They said, "We are people of strength and great might..(33)﴾ [al-Naml]..
11 Lawla: a conditional particle that does not govern, and indicates the negation of the response due to the presence of the condition. The conditional clause is nominal, and the predicate is necessarily omitted when it is a general existential verb, and when a detached pronoun of nominative form follows it. [al-Qamus al-Qawim]..
12 ﴿Why was there not a city that believed...(98)﴾: He, mighty and majestic, says: No city believed so that faith benefited it when the might of Allah descended upon them, ﴿except the people of Jonah..(98)﴾. It is said: when the punishment overshadowed them, and they thought it had drawn near to them, and they lost Jonah, Allah cast repentance into their hearts; they separated every female from her offspring, and they cried out, that is, raised their voices in invocation, to Allah for forty nights. So when He knew the sincerity of their repentance, He removed the punishment from them. ﴿..and We gave them enjoyment for a time (98)﴾: We did not hasten punishment upon them, and they enjoyed their lifespans in this world until the time of their death and the end of their lives. [Abridged Tafsir al-Tabari: pp. 241-242]..

Thus does the Truth, glory be to Him, make clear to us that there were many towns which believed only at the time of the punishment, and that this faith benefited none of them. But the people of Yunus, before the signs of the punishment and the might of it came, declared their faith, and the Truth, glory be to Him, accepted their faith, because He, glory be to Him, does not wrong His servants.

So whoever reaches the punishment and declares faith from within the punishment, it is not accepted from him. But whoever senses and perceives the first signs of the punishment and believes, the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, accepts it.

The word "lawla" (لولا): when you hear it, it is like "lawma" (لوما). When "lawla" enters upon a nominal sentence (جملة اسمية), its ruling differs from its ruling when it enters upon a verbal sentence (جملة فعلية). When it enters upon a nominal sentence, as in "lawla Zayd 'indaka la-ataytuka" (Had it not been for Zayd being with you, I would have come to you), it indicates that the non-occurrence of the coming is due to the presence of Zayd. But if it enters upon a verbal sentence, it is called a particle of urging and incitement (أداة تحضيض وحث), such as the saying of the Truth, glory be to Him:

﴿Why, then, did not a group from every section of them go forth, that they might gain understanding in the religion...(122)﴾ [al-Tawbah]: that is, it was required that from every group a number should go forth to study the matters of the religion.

And the Truth, glory be to Him, says here: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed...(98)﴾ [Yunus]. That is, had there been a town that believed before the punishment descended upon it, We would have saved it as We saved the people of Yunus; or it means: We would have loved for faith to arise from a town before the punishment came to it.

So the people of Yunus are here excepted, because they believed before the punishment came upon them.

There is another verse related to this story, in which the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And had he not been among those who glorify (Allah)(143), he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected(144)﴾ [al-Saffat]: that is, what prevented Yunus, peace be upon him, from remaining in the belly of the fish until the Day of Resurrection was his glorification (tasbih).

Here the Truth, glory be to Him, clarifies the exception that occurred for the people of Yunus when He says: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed, so that its faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world, and We let them enjoy for a time(98)﴾ [Yunus]. That is: the faith benefited the town of the people of Yunus before the punishment befell them.

For this reason the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿...When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world, and We let them enjoy for a time(98)﴾ [Yunus].

We know that the word "qaryah" (قرية, town) means a prepared place in which its people are settled. When a visitor passes by them at any time, he finds with them "qira" (قرى), that is, a meal (وجبة طعام).

And we find that whoever describes a homeland with many inhabitants uses the word "balad" (بلد), and such people possess food constantly. As for those who are a small minority in a place, usually they have only a little food, enough for themselves and for a visitor for one time.

Mecca the Honoured is called "Umm al-Qura" (mother of towns) because all towns visit it.

The town of the people of Yunus is named "Nineveh" (نينوى). The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, mentioned it in the account of his journey to al-Ta'if; it is the town of the righteous servant Yunus ibn Matta, and it is in Iraq, in the region of Mosul. It is Yunus of whom Allah, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And Dhu al-Nun, when he went off in anger...(87)﴾ [al-Anbiya']. The word "mughadib" (مغاضب) differs from "ghadib" (غاضب): the one who is angry (ghadib) becomes angry without anyone having provoked him, but the one who is mughadib is one whom another has angered.

Likewise the word "hajar" and "muhajir": the muhajir is one whom people have compelled to emigrate, but the one who hajar (left) went away by his own choice, far off.

So mughadaba (mutual anger) occurs from two sides, and it is called "mufa'alah" (a form expressing reciprocity).

The Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And Dhu al-Nun, when he went off in anger, thinking that We would not decree (anything) against him, then called out in the darkness: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers."(87)﴾ [al-Anbiya']. Our master Yunus, peace be upon him, was called Dhu al-Nun (Possessor of the Fish) because his name became associated with the fish that swallowed him.

We all know the story: when he called his people to faith, they disbelieved in him at the beginning, because the messenger, when he comes, comes to set right a corrupt life; those who live by corruption persecute him, because they want to keep the tyranny that allows them theft, embezzlement and the satisfying of the desires of the soul. When they did that to our master Yunus, peace be upon him, he went out in anger, that is, they angered him.

Mughadaba, as we said, belongs to the mufa'alah form and requires two parties, just as we explained that hijra (emigration) is also mufa'alah, because the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, did not abandon Mecca by himself; rather his people compelled him to emigrate, so they had a part in the act.

Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi says to this effect: "When you depart from a people who have resolved that you should not leave them, it is the departing ones who are they [i.e., the people]."
That is: if you live with a people and wish to part from them, and they have determined that you should remain with them, then the one who truly departs is these people.

After Yunus went out in anger, the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿...thinking that We would not decree (anything) against him(87)﴾ [al-Anbiya']. That is: he judged that the Truth, glory be to Him, would not constrict the wide earth for him, and would prepare for him another place other than the place of the hundred thousand or more whom Allah sent him to.

It was incumbent upon him to bear the harm that came from them toward him, but this thought, and thinking is the inclining toward a judgment, shows us that the opposition to his call was severe, provoking anger (تحفظ) and filling the heart with pain and weariness.

He had to prepare himself to face the hardships of the call.

The town to which Yunus, peace be upon him, was sent is the town of "Nineveh," which is mentioned in the course of a dialogue between the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the Christian boy "Addas" whom he met on his return journey from al-Ta'if.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, had gone to al-Ta'if to seek support from its people after his people had harmed him in Mecca, but he found no helper. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, sat near the wall of an orchard.

When the two owners of the orchard, Utbah and Shaybah, the sons of Rabi'ah, saw him and what he had met from the foolish ones, their kinship stirred for him. They called a Christian boy of theirs called Addas and said to him: "Take a cluster of this grape, place it on this platter, and take it to that man, and tell him to eat from it." Addas did so, then came with it and placed it before the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, and said: "Eat." When the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, put his hand in it, he said: "In the name of Allah," then ate. Addas looked at his face and said: "By Allah, this is not the speech of the people of this land." The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said to him: "From which land are you, Addas, and what is your religion?" He said: "I am a Christian, and I am a man from the people of Nineveh." The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "From the town of the righteous man Yunus ibn Matta." Addas said to him: "What do you know of Yunus ibn Matta?" The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "That is my brother; he was a prophet, and I am a prophet." Addas bent over the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, kissing his head, his hands and his feet.

When the two owners of the orchard asked Addas about this conduct of his, he said to them: "He told me of a matter that none knows except a prophet."

We know that the righteous servant, Yunus, peace be upon him, was affected, grieved and angered by his people's non-response to his message of faith, until they saw a cloud filling the sky and storms, and Allah cast into their hearts that these storms were the beginning of Allah's punishment upon them. They hastened to the wise men among them, who advised them that these were the precursors of the punishment, and said to them: "Upon you is to appease Yunus, for Allah, glory be to Him, is the One who sent him; so believe in him, that He may remove from you the distress."

The people hastened to faith in the Living who does not die, the Living when there is no living, the Sustainer, the Giver of life and the Causer of death.

The people of Yunus, peace be upon him, went to seek his pleasure; when he was pleased with them, they began to examine the injustices they had committed, to the extent that a man would tear down and demolish the wall of his house because in it was a stone he had misappropriated from a neighbour.
